content: # Damaris Cudworth Masham (1659-1708)

label: text
content: Damaris Masham (née Cudworth) was a moral philosopher who published two short treatises—A Discourse Concerning the Love of God (1696) and Occasional Thoughts in Reference to a Vertuous or Christian Life (1705) both of which bear the marks of John Locke's influence. $^{1}$ The following correspondence includes twenty-nine out of forty-five surviving letters between Masham and Locke from 1682 to 1688. There is also a selection of letters from Masham to the Genevan philosopher-theologian Jean Le Clerc and to the German philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, from the first few years of the eighteenth century. Taken as a whole, this correspondence reveals that while Masham constantly espoused a practicable ethical approach (a 'lived' Christianity), she also adapted and revised the epistemological foundations of her views. More specifically, in her letters it is possible to see a decisive shift away from an early adherence to the Platonist epistemology of her father Ralph Cudworth and his Cambridge colleagues John Smith and Henry More, toward a later commitment to Locke's empiricist theory of knowledge.

label: text
content: In her early letters to Locke, Masham defends certain Platonist views about divine intervention in the search for knowledge (3.1.2-7). In the first few months of their acquaintance, Locke and Masham engaged in a friendly epistolary quarrel about a book they had both been reading, the Cambridge Platonist John Smith's Select Discourses of 1660. They specifically discuss Smith's first discourse, 'A Præfatory Discourse concerning The true Way or Method of attaining to Divine Knowledge'. The main point of their dispute concerns whether or not Smith is an enthusiast, someone who bases knowledge of religious truths upon fancy and imagination alone, rather than reason. Locke affirms that Smith is an enthusiast; Masham denies it.

label: text
content: Recently, it has been suggested that Locke's letter about Smith's Discourses (3.1.3) sheds light on Locke's additions to the fourth and final edition of his

label: text
content: Essay Concerning Human Understanding of 1700. $^{2}$ For some years, Locke scholars have puzzled about why Locke added a new chapter 'Of Enthusiasm' (IV.xix) to this edition, and wondered how (if at all) this chapter fits into the wider philosophical project of the Essay. Philippe Hamou claims that Locke's letter to Masham reveals that he was long opposed to enthusiasm because of the connection between it and 'a brand of platonic anthropology assessing the human capacity for disincarnated knowledge'. $^{3}$ According to Hamou, this letter enables us to see how the chapter 'Of Enthusiasm' relates to another aspect of Locke's overall programme in the Essay: his goal to promote a new conception of human nature and to underscore the corporeal conditions of knowledge. In short, this correspondence shows that Locke might have been inspired to augment or refine his views on enthusiasm in light of Masham's remarks.

label: text
content: The correspondence also reveals that Masham herself was prompted to reconsider her epistemological commitments. In her letter of 16 February 1682 (3.1.2), Masham interprets Smith as saying that reason alone is not enough to make human beings become those 'new creatures' that St Paul mentions in Corinthians, those virtuous agents who live 'in Christ'. She suggests that something more than reason—a 'Higher Principle'—is required in order to attain such an exalted degree of moral perfection and divine knowledge; human beings are incapable of obtaining the highest pitch of moral perfection with 'meere Unassisted Reason' alone. Yet, as an avowed enemy of religious enthusiasts, she is reluctant to say that these views amount to enthusiasm. In response (3.1.3), Locke thinks that the so-called knowledge attributed to Smith's highest type of man ('the true Metaphysical and Contemplative man') is a species of enthusiasm. According to Locke, a firm persuasion of the mind might 'seeme as clear and operate as strongly as true knowledg', but if it is a notion about God or religion 'without any foundation of reason', then it does not qualify as divine knowledge, it must be dismissed as enthusiasm. In his second letter (3.1.6), Locke then suggests that enthusiasm is more properly classified as a kind of pathology or sickness than a species of knowledge. In ordinary, everyday life, he says, if someone is gripped by notions above and beyond reason (if they are persuaded of manifest contradictions and

Locke allows only that human reason might be indirectly assisted by God, insofar as God's providence bestows upon human beings the benefits of education, discourse, and contemplation. But in all such cases, he says, reason remains a natural human faculty—there is no direct supernatural assistance, as it were. $^{4}$

label: text
content: In response, Masham offers further reasons for denying that Smith is an enthusiast. In letter 3.1.7, she calls upon the authority of both Joseph Glanvill and Henry More to affirm her belief that God does directly assist those individuals who are prepared to be enlightened—but that acknowledging this assistance does not amount to enthusiasm. In his 1676 essay 'Against Modern Sadducism', Glanvill allows that God himself can engage in intimate communion with human beings and afford his 'Sensible Presence and Immediate Beatifick touch to some Persons so and soe Qualifyed'. We ought not to deny professions of this 'inward sense' of God, he says, simply 'because wee our selves do not feel them, nor can form any Apprehension of them'. $^{5}$ Masham evidently agrees with Glanvill. After quoting his text verbatim, she says that 'whatever therefore another professes to Experience in this kind How should I be able to Deny?' She further adds that we should not arraign those 'Sincere and Devout lovers of God and Vertue' or condemn them as

label: text
content: Persons who let themselves be imposed upon by there Immaginations and by the Suggestions of unbridled Phancie since thus long they do not quit there Reason; (as the Enthusiast does, who pretends to leave that light for a better (in which I suppose is there great Mistake, there being no suggestions of the Holy Spirrit but what are always agreable to, if not Demonstrable from Reason). (3.1.7; my italics)

label: text
content: Glanvill and More suggest that Masham does read Smith as subscribing to the divine direct assistance model of knowledge. But she does not regard this as enthusiasm because the divine sage need not abandon his reason in the acquisition of such knowledge. It is simply the case that God reveals to him certain truths—truths that are compatible with reason once the sage has obtained a higher spiritual disposition to receive them.

label: text
content: In her later published writings and in her letters to Leibniz (1704-5),however, Masham evinces a stronger commitment to Lockean empiricism. In her 1705 published work Occasional Thoughts, Masham explicitly asserts that human knowledge consists in the perception of the agreement or disagreement of ideas derived from sensory experience and reflection on the operations of the mind. Here there is no caveat that the highest form of knowledge requires direct supernatural assistance in addition to natural reason. Rather, in defining the parameters of knowledge, Masham considers only 'what light we receive from Nature to direct our actions'. Following Locke (Essay IV.xvii.2), she regards reason as the faculty that enables human beings to discover the agreement or disagreement of ideas, and to determine their assent accordingly. These same empiricist principles seemingly lie behind Masham's critique of Leibniz's notion of 'forms' in their 1704 correspondence. In one letter (3.3.2), Masham asks Leibniz to clarify what he means by 'forms' in his philosophy, since she cannot form a clear idea of the concept. Leibniz sometimes refers to them as 'primitive forces' or ' souls', and then also as 'constitutive of substances'; yet he denies that they are either matter or spirit. In response to Masham's request, Leibniz explains that his forms are the basic constituents of things: those unextended simple beings or ' atoms of substances' that have force as their essence (3.3.3). But still Masham insists that she has no 'positive idea' of the essence of these substances; she is simply unable 'to conceive an existence of that which is No Where' (3.3.4). In his Essay, Locke, too, maintains that we have no distinct idea of the real essences of what are commonly known as 'forms' (II.xxxi.6). We experience the simple ideas that constitute our complex idea of substance in general—of colour, weight, and hardness, for example—and we see that certain collections of ideas are joined together constantly, but we never get a distinct perception of the real internal essence of 'something called substantial form', he says. label: text
content: While Masham gradually revises and refines her epistemological outlook, she never deviates from her commitment to human sociability as the basis of a happy life. A constant theme of her writings is the need to find an even balance between human sociability and a suitable detachment from worldly concerns, in order to obtain happiness. Her early letters to Locke contain a continuous dialectic in which she attempts to reconcile these two opposing viewpoints: that is, a Christianized-Stoic philosophy of withdrawal from the external world, and a moral-religious ideal of human sociability and friendship with others. To live well, according to the ancient Stoics, moral agents must take control of their lives and determine their own life paths through the exercise of reason, and by desiring ends that are within their power to obtain. Masham supports this view when she says (only half-seriously) that

label: text
content: instead of thinking (as I used to do) that the Happyness of life consisted Principally in Societie, and Friendship, I now believe otherwise, and that to be Happy One must Care for Nothing, nor Nobody, Have no Friends, Love onely ones self, Nor never take any Concerne in the Good, or Ill, of other people whoever they be. (3.1.13)

label: text
content: One of the upshots of the Stoic viewpoint is that virtue lies in the perfection of one's reason and that virtue is the only good that one should pursue unconditionally, for its own sake. Society and friendship are neither good nor bad, but rather 'indifferents'. Masham expresses this sentiment when she says that 'Nothing in this World deserves Half the Care we usually Bestow upon it' and 'Happiness is not to be looked for in any thing without us' (3.1.14).

label: text
content: Nevertheless, Masham consistently comes back to the view that, while worldly detachment might be a laudable ideal, in practice human beings are constitutionally unable to live without loving and desiring their fellow creatures. In her letters to Locke, in particular, she frequently resigns herself to the fact that 'The Love of my Friends...and the Best Kinds of Usefull

Similar themes re-emerge in Masham's Discourse Concerning the Love of God, a critique of the extreme moral-theological views of Nicolas Malebranche, John Norris, and Mary Astell. Building on the ideas of Malebranche, Norris and Astell had argued that moral agents must not love their fellow creatures with a 'love of desire' (a desire to possess their beloved objects), but rather reserve their love of desire for God alone—the only being who could ever satisfy such desire. In response, Masham argues that human beings cannot remain completely impassive to one another's well-being. This is because they are naturally constituted to feel sociable passions, such as the desire to please others and a desire to have their love reciprocated in turn. To expect them to practice distinterestedness, she says, is like expecting fish to fly in the air—it is contrary to their natural constitution. $^{11}$ In her viewpoint, any practicable system of morality must acknowledge the inherent sociability of human beings. A religion that expects its adherents to withdraw from this world is a religion that few people will practice.

label: text
content: ## 3.1 Damaris Cudworth Masham and John Locke

label: text
content: John Locke and Damaris Masham probably first met in late 1681 through their mutual friend Edward Clarke. Shortly thereafter, Locke found some pretext to send Masham a letter. Thus began a correspondence that continued for many years, throughout Locke's period of exile in Holland from 1683 to 1689. Upon his return to England, Locke met with Masham and her husband Sir Francis, who eventually persuaded Locke to take up residence with them in their country manor house at Oates in Essex. Locke lived with the Mashams from 1691 till his death in 1704. The following correspondence includes a selection of twenty-nine letters between Locke and Masham from 1682 till 1688. $^{12}$

label: text
content: ## Sir

label: text
content: Be it under whatever pretence you please that you have sent me a letter, you ought not to feare that it should be ill taken, since nothing can be liable to a Misinterpretation that you say, who as I beleeve you would not really Deceive, so perhaps should you designe it you might not find it very easie, there being something necessarie besides Witt to make one succeed in it. You might therefore without any Apprehension have writt to me all that you Pleased. The Idea that I have formed of you in my Mind, could you have designed ill, would have secured me, and otherwise I am not unwilling to Contribute to your Diversion, in which I have found so agreeable an entertainment. But me-thinks Monsieur Scudery $^{13}$ being discarded as you say he is (for which I am very glad if he will not allow one to be pleased with the Esteeme of those for whom all the World has an esteeme) you should have let me knowne what new and better forms are introduced instead of those Antiquated ones of his which may be as convincing as Folded Arms and the sullens. I have beene told Lately by a Person for whom I have a greater Esteeme then for Voiture $^{14}$ that he is as much in the wrong too in making his Grand Cyrus and Aronces entertainine Clelia and Mandana with discourses so full of sence and write them letters so Witty and so Handsome, it being impossible as he said for those who love so to do. $^{15}$ You thought not of it I beleeve when you writt yours, nor do I desire that you should, should you ever write to me againe, for besides the difficultie that it would be to you to write otherwise then well there is nothing that I love better then good letters, and I would with all my Heart never receive an ill one upon any Account whatever. I am willing that expression of your Respect for me (if it be one) should be Defered till that revolution of time you speake of, when perhaps I as well as you may have different sentiments from those I now have. In the meane while permit me to think that it will be acceptable to you that I reckon you in the number of

label: footnote
content: 19 In this exchange, Masham and Locke principally discuss the third section of Smith's first discourse, 'A Præfatory Discourse concerning The true Way or Method of attaining to Divine Knowledge' in Smith, Select Discourses, pp. 1-21. There is evidence that Locke read Smith's other discourses as well, including his discourse on the immortality of the soul (Locke discusses this in a Journal entry), and another on superstition (he tells Masham that this is 'one of the best' he has read on this topic; see letter 3.1.3).

label: footnote
content: 20 In the third section of his 'True Way or Method of attaining to Divine Knowledge', Smith divides human beings into four ranks of being with respect to their methods of acquiring divine knowledge. (i) The lowest rank of being is made up of equal parts Soul' and Body': this man has a Knowledge in which Sense and Reason are so twisted up together, that it cannot be easily unraveled' (Smith, Select Discourses, p. 17). This man is easily steered by vulgar opinion and imagination; he has only an earthly conception of divine things. (ii) The second kind of man considers himself to be a soul rather than a body, and follows his reason in the search for divine knowledge. But although this man's soul rules his body—and he is therefore capable of 'more clear and distinct Opinions' than the first sort (p. 18]—in Smith's view, he nevertheless falls short of moral perfection because he fails to live up to 'divine' virtue. He practices human (moral and political) virtue alone. (iii) The third sort of man has a soul 'purged' of human virtue and is thus capable of 'flying off from the Body and Bodily passion' (p. 19). Yet if this man's knowledge is not tempered with humility, Smith warns, it could lead to an over-weaning self-love and the vices of pride, arrogance, and self-conceit. Thus, in his view, this man still falls short of true divine knowledge. (iv) By contrast, the fourth rank of man uses the best methods to attain knowledge of the divine and thus achieves the highest degree of perfection. He is 'the true Metaphysical and Contemplative man . . . who running and shooting up above his own Logical or Self-rational life, pierceth into the Highest life' (p. 20). In Smith's view, only this man is capable of attaining true knowledge of God.

label: footnote
content: $^{21}$ In a later letter (3.1.3), Locke explains his threefold division of men, as (i) those who think of themselves as body and mind alone and not soul (or spiritual substance); (ii) those who think of themselves as souls separate from the body, and who rely on 'vision' or imagination; and (iii) those who think of themselves as composed of both body and soul, and who rely on their reason.

label: footnote
content: 22 Masham interprets Smith as saying that reason alone is not enough to make human beings become those 'new creatures' that St Paul mentions in Corinthians, those creatures who live 'in Christ'. St Paul's precise remark is: 'Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ' (2 Corinthians 5:17-18).

Pray take care for the Future or I shall write you out of all Patience. You may be able to judge what I am like to do by this, since I am lame at present, and thought I could not have writt at all when I took the Pen in my Hand, having almost broke my Arm to day besides three or foure mischeifs more that I got all with a fall as I was standing still. Poore Mr C $^{24}$ —was almost scared out of his Witts at three Roomes distance and had not he come to my aid directed by the noise most certainly I had laine there till this time you see how carefull a Governess you have of me, that I neglect you notwithstanding all these disasters, but it is no more then you ought to expect from one who is so much your Friend and servant as Philoclea.

label: text
content: Pray if you expect any more letters from me let me know how I must direct them, since upon Mr Clerks asking his lady how, I undertook to tell and was corrected.

What unassisted reason can or cannot doe I cannot determin since I thinke the faculty its self <in its severall degrees of perfection> all the helps and improvements of it by education[,] discourse[,] contemplation or otherwise are all assistances from god and to be acknowledg to the goodnesse of his providence, but I thinke of reason as I doe of the sight an ordinary eye by constant $^{33}$ employment about any object may grow very accute in it the assistance of glasses may make it see things $<both>$ $^{34}$ better and at a greater distance but yet whatever is discerned by the eye however assisted is perceived <by> and comes under the naturall faculty of seeing, and soe what ever is known <however sublime or spirituall is known only> by the naturall faculty of the understanding and $^{35}$ reason, however assisted. content: 43 In the fourth edition of his Essay, Locke reiterates a number of the same points. God, he says, has bestowed upon our minds all the principles and foundations we require for knowledge. In particular, he has furnished us with reason as a natural means to arrive at knowledge of our duty to him. It is therefore absurd to think that God could ever require us to put aside this native faculty, and to accept something as true that would overturn all the principles and foundations he has given us. The enthusiast, however, requires us to do just that: to overturn reason and to substitute in its place 'the ungrounded Fancies of a Man's own Brain' (Essay IV.xix.3).

It would have been but Justice to have done this, since I believe that I owe much to your good wishes, I should be very glad if you knew how to increase my Obligation to them and that it were in there power too to restore me to as good a Humour as I am at present in an Ill one. I know not very well how it comes about, but I am extreamly Angry with my self, and have a strange Disposition to be soe with all the World besides. I wonder at you that knowing as you doe how subject I am to these kind of Fitts, at sometimes, that you would not so order it that I might have found some occasion of quarreling with you in case the fit were on me, and that I was disposed to it. But you have taken no care at all of that, so that in the present Humour that I am in I can find nothing at all to write to you about, unless it be to contrive a Quarrel against next time, which perhaps might succeed if I should tell you that it is my Authors fourth Division of Men that I all along meant, $^{46}$ which if you will call Enthusiasts in your next I shall think my self much concerned, and will resolve to take very Ill, this perhaps might do well enough, but however I do not tell you this, not being disposed to write any thing about the subject, nor knowing the Reason wherefore he calls this a fourfold kind of knowledge rather then as you say. But why would you put me upon this againe when I told you in my last that you must not? were you not affraid that in Revenge I should have asked your advice about makeing me a New Petticoate? Have sent you an Account of all the new Fassions that have beene since you left the Towne? told you what my new Manto $^{47}$ is made of? and a Thousand things more of the like Nature that I have all in store for you if you provoke me to it againe. For the present having better considered it and finding that my Letter is like to be sufficiently Impertinent without I resolve to reserve it till then, therefore pray take care and remember that you are only freely and Plainly to tell me your thoughts of my Author without ever examining mee about him, who $^{48}$ am so far from being able to explain His Opinions that I cannot give you an Account of my owne Actions which was the other thing that you desired of me, all that I know being onely that I got such a Fall as I told you of, but which ways I cannot for my Life immagine. You will see by this that I am the worst in the World at Answeareing Questions. The truth is, I have of late so Mortall an Aversion for it that twoo Hours Practice every night is so far from

That I have no Ill Opinion of the Platonists I confess, nor ought you to wonder at That seeing I have spent the Most of my Life amongst Philosophers of that Sect in whom I have always found the most Vertue and Friendship. $^{54}$ But as to what I writt to you certainly I did no more then onely tell you which way I thought we might come to quarrel, and not any thing else, and therefore you are very unkind in abuseing, as you have done, your Poore Governess so Cruelly. However not having now the leisure to be Angry I resolve for once to forgive you, though not without expecting that you should some time or other acknowledge your fault, which I think is but a Reasonable satisfaction. If you have any service to Command my Brother he is very readdy to Obey you. When He goes he does not yet know, but my Lord [Preston] talks of being in Paris before the Twenty fifth of this Month. I have received the Parcel you writt about and shall give it my Brother who will be sure to take care of it. I know not whether I ever told you that I writt to Dr C $^{55}$ —for you, from whom I received an Answeare not long since in which he presented his service to you. content: That which makes all these pretenses to supernaturall illumination farther to be suspected [delusion?] $^{74}$ to be mearely the effect and operation of the phansy is that all the preparation and ways used to dispose the minde to these illuminations and make it capeable of them are such as $^{75}$ are apt to disturb and depress the rationall power of the minde, but to advance and set on worke the phansy such are Fasting, solitude, intense and long meditation on the same thing, opium intoxicateing liquors, long and vehement turning round, <and so on> all which are used by <some or other of> those who would atteine to those extraordinary discoverys as fit preparations of the minde to receive them all which doe naturally weaken or disturb the rationall faculty and thereby let loose the imagination and thereby make the minde lesse steady in destinguishing, betwixt truth and $^{76}$ phansy but mistake as $^{77}$ crazy weake drunken or mad men doe one for the other.

label: text
content: It is neither to excess of Devotion in me, or defect of Charitie, that you ought to impute my silence, the occasions of which have been so many that I should tire both you and my self if I should recite them. I shall therefore onely assure you that they were unavoidable with which if you are not satisfyed I will next time send you a Catelogue of them, which I am sure (when you see) will be allowd by you for Just and Lawfull Impediments, although my want of Health will not be included in it, for your concerne of which I am extreamly Obliged to you, as also for your believeing that I have some Kind of Title to what I thought I had held merely from your free Gift, which Opinion how much soever you have confirmed in me I shall dispute with you no longer, but returne (since you have done so) to the Occasion of our former Difference which I designd not to have revived againe but onely to have knowne your thoughts of the following Discourses $^{82}$ which as I conceive have no Dependance on the Foregoing whatever the number of Sancho's Goats might have to the story he was teling his Master, $^{83}$ which I do not remember. content: any Disrespect to his Worth or Order was Fallible like other men, and that I am no more Obliged to believe as he does, then to reject for That reason any Opinion that is held by those of the Church of Rome, truth and Falshood being still the same from whom ever they are received, which I say not because I agree with the Jesuits in that Opinion of theres (if it be so) since I neither well know what they meane, nor think my self a fit judge of these things. But that I may Answeare the Authoritie of your Churchman with another, $^{85}$ there is one who giving reasons why there is no Communication betweene Good Angells and the Vertuous, gives it for one That God Himself affords his Intimacies and Converses to the better Souls that are prepared for it, That the Proud and Phantastick Pretences of the conceited Melancholists of this Age to Divine Communion had indeed Prejudiced many very Intelligent Persons against the beleefe of any such thing, They looking upon it but as a High flowne Notion of Warme Immagination as he acknowledges himself formerly to have done, But that having since considered it he is convinced, and does now abundantly believe That the Divine Spirit does afford its Sensible Presence and Immediate Beatifick touch to some Persons so and soe Qualified. $^{86}$ They are his owne words, but whether they amount to what was condemned in the Jesuits, or whether it be a Truth and Reallitie or not, is more then I know, and I only tell it you because it was from a Churchman who had the Reputation of Learning as well as yours, and was Esteemed a

label: footnote
content: 85 Masham refers to Joseph Glanvill's essay 'Against Modern Sadducism'.

label: footnote
content: 86 Masham paraphrases Glanvill's 'Against Modern Sadducism'. In this essay, Glanvill answers the sceptic's question that if there is indeed intercourse between evil spirits and wicked people, then why is there no correspondence between good angels and virtuous persons? Glanvill replies that this is because 'God himself affords his Intimacies, and converses to the better Souls, that are prepared for it' (Essays, p.29). He points out that

label: footnote
content: the proud and fantasticick Pretences of many of the conceited Melanchollists in this Age, to Divine Communion, have prejudiced divers intelligent Persons against the belief of any such happy vouchsafement; so that they conclude the Doctrine of Immediate Communion with the Deity in this Life to be but an high flown Notion of warm Imagination, and over-lushious self-flattery; and I acknowledge I have my self had thoughts of this nature. (p.29)

label: footnote
content: But upon reflection, he is now convinced that

label: footnote
content: the Divine Spirit affords its sensible Presence, and immediate Beatifick Touch to some rare Souls, who are divested of carnal Self, and mundane Pleasures, abstracted from the Body by Prayer and Holy Meditation; spiritual in their Desires, and calm in their Affections; devout Lovers of God, and Vertue, and tenderly affectionate to all the World; sincere in their Aims, and circumspect in their Actions; inflarged in their Souls, and clear in their Minds: These I think are the dispositions that are requisite to fit us for Divine Communion. (p.30)

label: footnote
content: Glanvill allows that God himself can engage in intimate communion with human beings and that God affords his 'Sensible Presence and Immediate Beatifick touch to some Persons so and soe Qualified' (p.30).

label: text
content: more then ordinaryly Ingenious Man. As for my self being not in the number of those fitly Qualified Persons I can be no judge of it, Things of inward sense being not to be Denyed (as Hee says) because wee our selves do not feell them, nor can form any Apprehension of them, Nor are they to be Judged of by the noetical $^{87}$ exercises of speculative understanding, but by the Sentient and Vital Faculties. $^{88}$ Whatever therefore another professes to Experience in this kind How should I be able to Deny? And Provided that they Act not nor Admit any thing but what they can give a Rational Account of, That they Pay a Universal Obedience to all the laws of God, and that they believe the Holy Scriptures I do not see any Reason why there opinion should be quarreled with, or themselves Condemned as Persons who let themselves be imposed upon by there Immaginations and by the Suggestions of unbridled Phancie since thus long they do not quit there Reason; as the Enthusiast does, who pretends to leave that light for a better (in which I suppose is there great Mistake, there being no suggestions of the Holy Spirrit but what are always agreeable to, if not Demonstrable from Reason) But if to any this great Priviledge be Vouchsafed I do not know why it may not as well be so to all who are as Sincere and Devout lovers of God and Vertue, and who do Faithfully adhere to that light which they already have, of which I suppose there are many amongst the most Barbarous Nations and Professors of the Wildest Religions in the World, as well as reall Enthusiasts everywhere, as I suppose those Ricaut and Monsieur Berniere $^{89}$ speake of might bee, but in the number of whom I did not indeed believe Mr S[mith], looking upon the designe of that whole Discourse in General as no other then to recommend Puritie of Life as the onely true way of attaining to Divine Knowledge $^{90}$ in which are made the greater advances by how much the more the Mind is purged from all Impuritie, there being a Natural Cohesion of Truth with impolluted Souls, and also, as Dr More says, a Principle Antecedaneous to Reason which he calls Divine Sagacitie which is onely Competible to Persons of Pure and Unspotted Minds and without which Reason is not succesfull in

label: footnote
content: $^{87}$ Noetical] purely intellectual.

label: footnote
content: 88 Again, Masham paraphrases Glanvill's essay: 'I saw how little reason there is in denying Matters of inward Sense, because our selves do not feel them, or cannot form an apprehension of them in our Minds: I am convinced that things of gust and relish must be judged by the sentient and vital Faculties, and not by the noetical Exercises of speculative Understandings' (Essays, p. 30).

label: footnote
content: $^{89}$ Paul Rycaut and François Bernier, the authors mentioned in Locke's previous letter (3.1.6).

label: footnote
content: 90 In the first section of his discourse, Smith declares that 'Purity of Heart and Life, as also an Ingenuous Freedome of Judgment, are the best Grounds and Preparations for the Entertainment of Truth' (Select Discourses, p.1).

label: text
content: ## 3.1.8 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 6 May 1682; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 91-2.

label: text
content: May the 6th

label: text
content: Though I am at this time in a very Unusual Humour, and not at all disposed to write Letters, Yet seeing no likelihood of being soone in $^{93}$ any other, I have resolved however to tell you soe, that I may not any more runn the risque of provokeing you to Anger, which I would not willingly do, notwithstanding what you say of your having no good Facultie at Chideing, $^{94}$ to which if you had but the lest inclination in the World you could certainly never doe with mee at a better time then now, Since the Dispensation $^{95}$ I am at present got

label: footnote
content: 91 Masham refers to Henry More's views in the preface to his Collection of Several Philosophical Writings. In a marginal note, More defines divine sagacity as 'a Principle antecedaneous to successful Reason in Contemplations of the highest concernment' (Collection, p. vii). He says that

label: footnote
content: intellectual success therefore is from the Presence of God, who does . . . move all things in some sort or other, but residing in the undefiled Spirit moves it in the most excellent manner, and endues it with that Divine Sagacity I spoke of, which is a more inward, compendious and comprehensive Presentation of Truth, ever antecedaneous to that Reason . . . and is truely that wisedom which is peculiarly styled the Gift of God, hardly compatible to any but to persons of a pure and unspotted mind. (p. ix)

label: footnote
content: He also speaks of 'the natural cohesion of Truth with an impolluted Soul' (p. ix).

label: text
content: into would not so much as permit me to quarrel with you again, but has within these Six Days made me the Meekest, Humblest, Quietest, Creature you ever saw. Let People say what they will, or Doe what they will, I take all with Submission, and like those whom Use and Custom has hardened am become almost capable of indureing all things. Should you therefore take a Phancie to be Angry with me without a cause, Or should you interpret the best intentions I could have Perversly, Or what would be more Cruel then either of them should you have such Thoughts of me as I should believe Inconsistent with that Esteeme which necessarily accompanies a Durable Friendship, All this would be no more then I have beene taught to suffer, and that without murmuring. You will not I suppose think that I have beene able to be brought to this without having a Profound Indifference for all things in the World besides, and it is certain that at this time I have soe. I have beene thinking therefore that the best improvement I can make by my Misfortunes will be to take advantage of my Temper and turne a Stoick. $^{96}$ It is now certainly if ever that I shall be able to do it, since being not by Nature Quarrelsome I should never have the Power to fall out with the World if That did not first begin with mee. You must not now therefore expect that I should any longer Pursue a Discourse which perhaps would not be approved by the Philosophers of that Sect which I am going to embrace, besides that if I would I should find it almost impossible, since my Afflictions have had that effect upon my Memory that I remember not any thing of that Letter but the Subject, nor scarsely any thing else that is above Nine Days Old, and therefore since wee are so far agreed I think it will be best to end that Dispute. I do not expect any more then you that the World should be all of one Mind, neither do I desire that they should, provided that I my self could but be soe. But I am at present so far from that, that I believe I have not for these many Days changed my Dress so often as my thoughts, nor knowne any thing so little as my owne Heart. There are but twooo things in the World that I can find to which I remaine always Constant, and those are the Love of Vertue, and my Friends, whom in all tempers I experience that I equally regard, and value, and Therefore should the Phantasticalness and Inequalitie of my Humour, which you will every Day discover more then other (besides a Thousand other Faults and Weaknesses) make you to be less one of them, then now you are, I assure you I must make greater advances in Stoicisme then I feare I shall

label: footnote
content: 96 a Stoick] an adherent of Stoicism, the philosophy that we should cultivate a radical detachment from all external circumstances over which we have no control.

label: text
content: ## 3.1.9 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 23 May 1682; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 93-4.

label: text
content: May the 23d

label: text
content: I onely write to you now to let you know that you have a Governess who cannot forget you. Otherwise being so lately come to a new place, $^{97}$ Haveing parted with so many Persons who are Deare to me, and Being now with others who are to leave me within these three Days, I find not my self at all in a Humour of writing any more then I was the last time, nor of being much better pleased with my self or the World, although for the designe of turning a Stoick I begin to suspect that it will not doe, notwithstanding that I have just Bought Anthony LeGrand of the Passions, $^{98}$ and am reading over Seneca $^{99}$ the second time, who is so far from having taught me more Patience then I had before that in an Houres reading Hee has awakened mee out of that State of Insensibleitie that I seemed to be in, and Provoked me to Cholor $^{100}$ above Half a Dosen times. What amends he may make me in his succeeding Discourses I know not but this has been a great Disappointment to me Hitherto who incounterd him as an Old Friend almost sent by Providence for my releife. But Seneca I suppose is still the same that he was three Yeares agoe, and it is I that am altered, who cannot Deny the Changableness and Inconstancie of my Nature, how bad a Character soever I give of my self by it, nor alter it, how great soever the Inconveniences are that I suffer by it and the Mistakes that it runs me into. It is not above a Fortnight since that I believed I could have lived as well pleased in one place as another, that I stood not in need of any Body, and that I was a whole World to my self, and now I experience so much the Contrary that Methinks I am Divided into as many Parts as there are Persons that I love, and that it is intollerable to live in a Place where

For Heavens sake if you know such another place as this is tell me some what of it, and of some Body that ever sufferd as I do, and if there should never have beene any such I beseech you however dont scruple telling me so Pleaseing a Falshood, since I love some companion in all Conditions, and Have not Vertue enough to wish that I may be the onely Unfortunate. label: text
content: ## 3.1.10 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 10 June 1682; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 95-6.

label: text
content: June the 10th

label: text
content: What ever you think of me I assure you it is not my Way to Complaine without Reason, and you may always conclude that I am certainly in a bad Humor whenever I tell you so, since I never accuse my self falsly of things which I cannot believe it should be to my advantage to be thought Guiltie of. However since you believe that an Ill Humor may sometimes be agreeable for the sake of Varietie, I may not perhaps henceforwards take so much care to avoid it as I have hitherto done, since the desire of pleaseing my Friends is always much more Prevalent with mee then that of being pleased my self. But pray remember now that it is You who have put me upon this, and that if you should find any Ill effects of it hereafter you will have no body to thank for it but Your self. At present I am well enough pleased, and believe notwithstanding what you say to the Contrary That I am not onely as good a Physitian as I am a Philosopher but something a better one, since not being able to returne to my Usual Humour by the exercise of all the Reason I was Mistress of, I have at length found out another expedient to effect it, which has been by Diverting it another way, in which I have succeeded by injoyning my self a certaine task in the Performance whereof I take much sattisfaction, but you being my Puple, and not I yours, I think I am not Obliged to give you any Account what that is. It suffices that you kno it has proved so effec tual that I question whether the Aire of London could have beene much more so, notwithstanding that if it were convenient I could not forbeare having

label: text
content: a most Vehement Desire to see divers Persons who are there. I doubt not at all but you find it as agreeable a Place as you left it, if every body that uses to be there be so still, except mee. However if it be not so, I feare I shall not be very sorry for you, since how much soever I am your Friend I must confess that I cannot surmount that infirmitie of my Nature which makes me on such occasions as these glad when other People are no better pleased then my self, and upon this account to confess the truth to you it would have beene much to my satisfaction to have had you have continud at O[xford] still. $^{101}$ You cannot easielie immagine what a Tenderness the Parellel betweene our twooo Conditions was begining to have begot in me for you. But now considering you quite otherwise with some Kind of Envy as one Happier then my self I find I know not how that that new sort of Affection for you Insensibly decreases and that you will be to me but just what you use to bee. For after all that I have told you of my good Humour you must know that Philosopher like I owe it wholly to my self, finding it convenient at this time to scorne to be beholden to any thing without me for it, $^{102}$ not having so much as that conversation you mention to contribute any thing towards it, so that the present state that I am in you may conceive to be rather that of Quiet and contentment, then of any mightie extraordinarie Delight or Pleasure. But as I take it that is most Stoical, and therefore as it should be, that designe being not yet quite abandoned. And now should I conclude my letter but that I have a request to make to you which though not very Philosophical according to my present Genius Yet considering that you love Varietie, and that it will be agreeable to a Certaine Humor of mine which usually takes place once in Twenty foure Hours, I shall not Omit it. It is (heareing that you go soone to Tunbridge) $^{103}$ that you will for my sake be as Impertinent there as ever you can, and that as a Consequent of that you will take care to Informe me in all the little News of that Place, As who is the most celebrated Beautie there, who loves who, and all That, which it is needless to tell you. In the meane time I have another Favour to beg of you in the doing of which you will much Oblige me too, and that is, that you would instruct mee a little How it is that one ought to write Letters of Consolation, especially those in which one beleaves there is not much of it needfull. I have such a one lays upon my Hands now which I would faine

content: ## 3.1.11 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 1 July 1682; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols.97-8.

label: text
content: July the first $^{104}$

label: text
content: Methoughts it was very pleasantly spoken on that occasion that it was by a certaine Lord a Friend of yours, $^{105}$ That it much pleased him to see that the Learned could be Out, and the most Knowing Mistaken, as well as others. I remember that I was then of the same opinion, and it is since, from a Phancie not very unlike it, that I have so much desired that you should be Impertinent. $^{106}$ Wonder not therefore any more (I beseech you) at a request that I renew to you againe now that you are going to the Waters, $^{107}$ where I wish you all the Pleasure that you can expect or desire, and should have done it something sooner but that I thought I might have sent you a Book before you went which my Brother has sent me for you, but which I have not yet received. When I do I shall take the Pleasure now of reading it before you see it, although I have already designed my self so much Work of that Kind that I know not when I shall finish it, and All to keepe my self in a good Humor, which yet methinks I need not take so much Pains to doe, since I find the Good Innocent Aire is like to have all the blame of my Ill ones. You are very Obliging indeed in laying all the fault upon that, since you make me thereby perfectly Gui[l]tless, But however I think in Honor I ought not to let it suffer Unjustly and therefore do assure you whatever your Opinion of it is, that it is as quiet an[d] Harmless an

label: text
content: You see now that you have a Governess that will be strictly Just though to her owne disadvantage. I hope therfore this letter will restore me to your good Opinion and Attone for all the Envy and Ill Humour you found in my last, for which the truth is I cannot repent, that being a thing which you Know is naturally my Aversion, and Besides that if I should ever do it I would willingly do it once for all which I find would be impossible to do now, that you are going to Tunbridge, and that it is not yet long Vacation. However I assure you this that mine is an Envy after a new Mode which will never hinder me from wishing you those Pleasures which I grumble for the want of, nor from being Sir

label: text
content: ## 3.1.12 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, c. 14 August 1682; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 99-100.

label: text
content: Haveing as I think formerly Confest to you that it was my Custome very often to prevent the Accusations of my Friends by begining first with them when I knew my self to be Guiltie, I shall not Therefore do so now. Although I could take my Choise at this time of three or foure several ways that would all serve to prove the fault Yours that I have not writt to you all this while. But besides this, I have a Mind to let you see too, that under the Name of Friends, which in Conformitie, I as well give to People that I do not much Care for as to those that I doe, are Comprised a number of People whome $\mathrm{I}^{108}$ treat very Differently, and whom for Convenience sake I divide into foure or five Orders or Distinctions of Friends, finding my self capable of so many Different Degreese of Friendship. Not to Consider then in which Rank of them you stand, I do undoubtedly find you in the number of those to whom I look upon my self as under an Indispensible Obligation of useing sinceritie. I shall therefore very freely acknowledge my self faultie, assureing you that if I had not a great Opinion of your Goodness I should hardly know how to ask Pardon for so much Rudeness

content: and Incivilitie as I have beene Guiltie of. Not but that perhaps I could say something that might extenuate a great part of it by letting you know that we have had those here to whom I was obliged to pay a Tiresome Attendance That I have beene very much Indisposed with an Unusual Paine in my Head, and still am soe, Besides that I have twice beene out of the Towne, with other things of this kind. But because that I Naturally have an Aversion to all Excuses, and Excuse Makers, and am willing to increase the Obligation I shall owe you, I shall not insist upon these things, nor indeavour to take from the Merrit of that Faith, whose Impliciteness is not of less Value in Friendship, then it is in Religion. But who can assure me that you are not a Heretick in both? For the last it is I think your owne Concerne wholly, and therefore I shall Leave it wholly to you, but for the first it is at Present become so much Mine that I Beg it of you, who though I am very Carefull in Denouncing Damnation, must needs assure you, that this is no Venial Sin, $^{109}$ at lest I could produce a great Author or twoo for it, who methinks in this matter should be of some Authoritie with you, Though it would indeed be the more Obliging to beleieve me upon my owne, who I perceive you think may be One, in time, if I am not Pretty well towards it already. But since the Conceptions of Friendship for <such only are mine> (as I take it) hold no agreement with Baby Clouts $^{110}$ methinks that Curiositie which you once had to have inquired more narrowly after them, should still Continue, Nor should you so easilie be put off by an excuse which I cannot allow for a just one, in the Lady who made it, $^{111}$ who as I have beene informed, does not use to be prevented by such Occasions from doing things of the like Nature. But you are resolved I see still to put me in need of the Old Remidie from which I have but Lately received a Cruel Diversion, and therefore to Answer your question the best that I can, It is now so long since I writt to you last, that I know not very well what I did then, But for this Present time, and for a good while past, I do assure you, that I have not only Thought, but have found it some Paine to me, to doe any thing else beside thinking, which should I give a stricter Account of it, would be found none of the lest causes of my not Writeing to my Friends. I should presume too much upon your Friendship should I entertaine you with things in which you could take no Part, but what your Natural Goodness, and Compasion would give you, and therefore I shall onely tell you in short, that I am upon the point of loseing in a Brother $^{112}$ the Dearest Person in the

label: text
content: World to me, to whose Advantage (as I am perswaded) I have Sacrificed all Considerations of my owne Satisfaction, in Consenting to a Voiage from which I have but small Hopes of seeing him returne. If you have ever knowne what it is to Love so Tenderly as I doe, or knew but Half my Weakeness, You would not doubt but that I have had many thoughts before I could come to such a Resolution, and as many since I have done it, which are so little Pleaseing to me that you would lay the Greatest Obligation in the World on me if you could teach me to live with out any at all. As for your second question whether I think that the Lady who writt to you $^{113}$ Left her Heart at London, or No, when she came from thence, If she has Witt, as you say she Has, I do assure you, that she did not, But though perhaps (for all your Complement) she may not have very much, Yet I assure you that those who know her, doe her the Honour to beleeve, that she takes as much Care of her Heart, as many Wiser People. However it be she nevertheless thinks her self much Obliged to that Friend of Hers that would be so Carefull of it for her, and I dare not be assured, that it may not be an occasion of makeing her more Negligent for the Future, then she has ever beene for the time that is past;—But to returne to my self, Is it possible that you should be Angry with your Governess, and that for no other Cause but not reading your Books. I must Confess indeed that beleeveing at present I should have no use of the Art of Navigation, $^{114}$ the first look into it Discouraged me from proceeding farther, But if you are of an other Mind, and think it is as usefull to me, as some here do Architecture, and Trigonometri, I shall set about the understanding of them all, as fast as I can. In the meane time My Deare Pupil Pardon my Error if I have beene in one, and excuse all the other faults of your Faithfull Humble Servant

label: text
content: And that I was much better Pleased to heare news of You from the Elizian Feilds, $^{115}$ then I should have beene from either France, Germanie, or Holland. Although I am very sorry to hear that you Cannot be Happy in a Place where all the World is so. And yet perhaps, if the Truth were knowne, you are not much Otherwise, or surely so small a thing as my Idea in your Mind, could never have put you in so good Humour. If it did, I must needs think (whatever you tell me to the Contrary) that Experience has convinced you, that (at least) there are some things that are better in the Idea, then in themselves (However as Good) for certainly my Real Presence could not have done more at that Time then that did, if it were as you say, and therefore I think it will be better to let you Continue still in Elizium by your self, then run the Hazard of an Unprofitable Journey to keepe you Company there, Besides that I am not of the Mind that it is so great a Misfortune to want a Companion, For in this long time since I writt to You last, in which some People perhaps would have changd there Minds above Twentie times, I have changed mine once, and instead of thinking (as I used to do) that the Happyness of life consisted Principally in Societie, and Friendship, I now believe otherwise, and that to be Happy One must Care for Nothing, nor Nobody, Have no Friends, Love onely ones self, Nor never take any Concerne in the Good, or Ill, of other people whoever they be. According therefore to this Opinion you cannot be Unhappy, and I am just now so mightilie perswaded that it is a Right One, that I am upon the very point of resolving immediatly to indeavour all that I can to reduce it into Practice, although I should have beene very glad to have had it received your approbation first, which I dare say you would give it upon farther Consideration, there being a Thousand Conveniences in it that I have not time now to Mention, who then shall never trouble you with such long letters as this, at lest if to do so, it be necessarie to have either Witt, or Kindness. For as for the First, I have it not already, and for the second, to be sure Then I shall not, nor can you complain of me for it, when all the World besides will be alike indifferent to me, and since that till then I shall always be very much

label: text
content: ## 3.1.14 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 28 November 1682; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fol. 109.

label: text
content: I have at Present some extraordinarie occasions of Business, and am otherwise so little Disposed to write, that did I not feare you would think me sullen, or Rude, or something or other almost as Bad, I should not let you heare from me till I came to London, where I shall be on Thursday sevennight, staying here $^{117}$ this Weeke to see the solemnities of Sir John Finches Funeral over First for whom all here, are true Mourners. $^{118}$ On Thursday next He will be brought to this Place and Buryed by Sir Thomas Bains, whom He Buryed Here, not above four Months since. $^{119}$ I have not time now to give you none of my Thousand Reasons and it is like have forgot many of them by this time, But I am sure I shall always know one good one to make me think nothing in this World deserves Half the Care we usually Bestow upon it, and that Happiness is not to be looked for in any thing without us. I thank God I have never in my Life beene much of any other Mind, and therefore it is not any Disappointment that makes me more so now then ever, no more then that in some Melancholy Humour I am faln out with the World, so that I would not have you expect if ever you see me againe you should find me worse Company then I use to be, or less then I was, your Friend,

label: text
content: Philoclea.

label: text
content: I suppose you will perceive that I am in hast and accordingly excuse me for what I know not well what I write.

label: text
content: ## 3.1.15 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 16 June 1684; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 114-5.

label: text
content: Could I have knowne that it would have beene more Acceptable to you to have done otherwise, you have Reason enough to beleive that I would not have beene Silent, Nor have sent you other Peoples Words without any of my owne to Accompanie them; my Fault therefore if I was Guiltie of any, I Appeal to your self was of Invincable Ignorance, and as such, Knowing you to be Just, I do without asking it, Venture to assure my self of your Pardon; As for mine you certainly long since had it, since I have almost forgot those Resentments you tell me of, and every thing else that was in that Letter; though I thought I had rather expresed my self in it to be in a very good Humour, then an Ill one, and that I was better Sattisfyed with my Solitude at that time, then I had of a long while before beene: I am now going to it againe, and wish that I may be but as well Pleased with it now, as I was then; The little Pleasure that I have taken of late in any Company has made it extreamly desirable to me, Yet I indeavor what I can, not to lose all my old Aversion to it, since I find the Cure to be much worse then the Disease, it being oweing to the Greatest Discontent that I ever yet received, and to the most Real Disgust of the World, occasioned by the Misfortune, or extreame Folly more truely, of a Person that has always beene to me the Dearest Part of my self, Hee to whom you was Pleased to write, or Designe it, about a Yeare since, which Letter (if you did) hee had not received when he writt His to mee which came very lately. $^{120}$

label: text
content: I am now I hope Absolutely Cured of Promiseing my self any great Pleasure in this World, though it depended upon so many Contingences before, that I think I deserved to be Punished for but Flattering my self with an Imagination that it may be it might bee.

label: text
content: Inclinations so little Sutable to this, and so unlike ever to be Gratifyed; Though if I could have Faith enough to believe Helmonts Opinion, $^{122}$ and Could with as strong a Fancie conceit my self to have beene Methuselah $^{123}$ (as its said a great Philosopher did Him self to have beene One who was Slaine at the Seige of Troy) $^{124}$ I think it might do all out as well, and I could not sure then want Patience to Compleate my Thousand Yeares either now, Or in any other Age of the World; The Truth is, with the Present I have beene much more out of Conceite for these Ten Days, and feare I shall continue so, then when I had the Designe that you Know of turning Stoick; I see more then ever, that it is a Base, False, Foolish World; and that Vertue, Honour, and Friendship, are but Names in it, Whilst People sell theire Honestie for Imaginarie Profit, and theire Happiness for the Senceless Reputation of being Wise. But this is our World, and as it Appears to me in the Discontented Humour that I am in; I should be very glad to heare a Better Account of yours; which if you cannot give, Pray inform me a little about your Neighbors in Frieze Land, $^{125}$ the L'abadies, $^{126}$ Since though I be ever so far Distant from them, it would much Reconcile me to the World to know that there were but somewhere in it a better sort of People then those where I am; I desire therefore that you will tell me what theire Manner of liveing is; and Whether it be that, or any Peculiar Principle, or Opinion, in theire Religion which Unites them together; What that is; Whether they be Learned, or Unlearned; and whether in theire Lives, and Conversation one amongst Another they do really differ from the rest of the World, and do appeare to have more true Honestie amongst them.

label: text
content: As for the Inquiries which you make at the end of your Letter I can onely refer you for the first of them to the General Fame that has been in all Ages Concerning that Matter, which I think has spoke Loudly in theire Praise. As for my self, If I may be Allowed to make a Judgment of what I was then by

label: footnote
content: 122 In his Two Hundred Queries (1684), Francis Mercury van Helmont (1614-98) claims that God has granted all human beings one thousand years in which to repent for their sins. Out of fairness, van Helmont argues, those who died without repentence before the coming of Christ must be given a chance to redeem themselves; they must be born into the world again, to live out their millennium. To account for this, van Helmont puts forward his doctrine of the revolution (recurrence) of souls.

label: footnote
content: 123 In Genesis 5:27, Methuselah is reported to have lived to the age of 969.

label: footnote
content: 124 The ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras purportedly claimed that in a previous life he was Euphorbus, the great warrior slain by Menelaus in the siege of Troy. Van Helmont refers to the Pythagorean doctrine of metempsychosis in queries 192 and 193 of his Two Hundred Queries.

label: footnote
content: 125 Frieze Land] Friesland, a province of the Netherlands. By this time, Locke was in exile in Holland.

label: footnote
content: 126 Labadies] Labadists, a Protestant sect founded by Jean de Labadie (1610-74), and then based at Walta Castle in Wiuwert in Friesland. Among their adherents in the 1670s was the Dutch philosopher Anna Maria van Schurman (1607-78), author of Eukleria, or Choosing the Better Part (1673), a defence of Labadism.

label: text
content: ## 3.1.16 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 25 August 1684; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 116-17.

label: text
content: Whether the World was always the same it is, or no, in its Antediluvian State, or since, I leave to the Author of the new Theorie to determine, $^{128}$ But this I am very Confident of that you are still the same you always was ever since I Knew you, and that no Change of Climate or any thing else is able to make one in your Humour. It is not to your Praise that I tell you this, Since to Confess the Truth I made Account so Melancholy a letter as mine (at lest one that expresed me with so much Reason Afflicted) should for those few moments that you were thinking of me have a little suspended that Pleasantness which is so Natural to you, and I should yet quarrel with you for its not doing so, did I not Justly Apprehend that you would excuse your self by laying all the Blame upon Astrea, $^{129}$ and tell me over againe that Friendship, as well as Vertue, and Honour, being of Her Retinue, forsook the World when she did; If it be so wherefore Should I come into Freezeland? and what is there to be found There that is not to be had as well where I am? Notwithstanding the Character which you have given of the Labadies I acknowledge that I like very well, But should have thought it an Excellent One had not the Notion I then had of them been quite altered since I writt to you last, I having beene informed since (but how Rightly I know not) that they are so far in Realitie as well as in theire Pretences (if that be true which you say of them) from being

content: better then others, that they are indeed so much worse as under a show and Appearance of Religion there are not really greater Libertines in the World; like some Here in England formerly of whom I suppose you have heard, They were a sect in Particular very Prevailing with the Women of the Place, $^{130}$ and therefore notwithstanding your Advise I think it will behoove me to be Very Cautious how I enter into Acquaintance with the like till you have made further Inquiries Concerning them, although I partly suspect alreadie in what you did write that you had a mind to try how far my Credulitie might be Abused. In the meane time I find my self much more Disposed to see Holland, then Freezland; and can't but fancie that the Sight of a Place where Love, and Business, may be so well reconciled, is as much worth my Curiositie as that of the Labadies; and Yet how good Opportunitie soever I may ere long have of doing so, I shall scarse be encouraged to it by all that you have yet said, There being Convenient Lime Treese, and Canals Large enough, if there be occasion for them, much nearer hand, Unless you let me know that there are some Idle People there were [sic] you are besides your self, Business you know, being as Mr Cowley says, the Thing which I of all things Hate; $^{131}$ and that I have a Perswasion that All There have nothing else in them no more in theire Heads, then in theire Hearts; If you say that this is an Errour, and can find me but any Acquaintance such as you Promised me in France I may Possibly ere it be long come and learne some of those fine Dishes you talk of, Otherwise they will be no Temptation to me not having any Designe at Present to become a Housekeeper, any more then a Labadie. How Time may Dispose me either way I know not, For for the last I would not have you think by any thing that I have said that I am so Prejudiced against them that I should not be willing to heare any Ill that I have heard of them Refuted, and to entertain a good Opinion of them. I do also much desire to see the Book you tell me of, and Wonder you have found no Opportunitie of sending it me all this While, as it may be you may that I have beene thus long of writeing to you, The Reasons of which I cannot give you without telling you a great many sad stories which I know cannot be Pleasant to any Body, and which would

label: footnote
content: 130 I am unable to identify this religious sect 'in England formerly'. Masham possibly refers to some controversy involving former members of the Religious Society of Friends, the Quakers. Women were active and vocal participants in the early Quaker movement. In 1683 alone (the year before Masham's letter), Elizabeth Bathurst published her defence of women's preaching, The Sayings of Women, Anne Docwra her Epistle of Love, and Dorcas Dole Once More a Warning.

label: footnote

label: text
content: ## 3.1.17 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 8 October 1684; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 118-19.

label: text
content: Though the quarrel that I had with the World when I writt to you from L[ondon?] was not of the Nature of those (as most Commonly they are) after which People love it but the Better, But Reasonably enough Grounded to be Lasting Yet has not my Desire of retireing from it beene of late any thing so great as it uses to be; Not that I am not as much as ever I was a Stoick; and less that the Stars have informed you aright; Since on the Contrarie for the first I cannot but think my Courage (for so it is) an effect of my improvement in that Philosophy, And for the last do assure you I am so far from any such thoughts that I have beene in much greater Likelihood both from my owne Inclination, and the Perswasion of others, (though for different Reasons) of makeing a Resolution never to have any such whilst I live. But Considering that if I did so I should for that very Reason have had an Invincible Temptation of doing otherwise, I have with much ado forborne, and am now so far come off from it as to have a great deal the better Opinion of your Neighbours in Freezeland for not doing so neither, Of whom a more Particular Account would have beene very Pleaseing to me, that do not Perhaps as you say inquire onely out of Curiositie, since though I am growne more Hardie, Or thro the Continuance of the Evills I complained of less sensible, and so can better indure this Wicked World then formerly Yet it follows not from thence that I always will do so, and therefore I may (notwithstanding your Opinion to the Contrary) in time Possess the Place that you have taken up for me, Besides that you have given me a New Temptation to do so, since most Certainly if ever I come to be Perfectly reconciled to Matrimonie againe I shall have an extreame Desire to Marry a Labadist, and be one my self for that very

content: Who Know no Interest Contrary to their Inclination; and Who are Wiser either in Marrying, or not Marrying, then to Rate theire Happiness by the Estimation that others make of it more then theire owne. It is thus that I fancie them as to this matter, and am almost in Love with some unknowne Brother alreadie; But when you write next you must let me know whether or no I am not mistaken in them, as also whatever else you can think of that concerns theire Manner of liveing, though by the Way if they are so shy of informing those who inquire onely out of Curiositie I doubt you had not much Conversation with them, since whatever it was that Carryed you into Freezeland I suppose you would not impose upon them so much as to Perswade them that it was with any Designe at all of Becomeing Better; though some way or other it has Certainly beene Advantageous to you, since I cannot but Fancie by your Letter that you have learnt more Scripture there then ever you Knew in your whole life before, whom I little thought once would ever have writt me a letter not to be understood without turning to St Paul, and St Peters Epistles.

label: text
content: The Booke you sent me (for which I returne you my Thanks) I received but a Week since, and have yet had but very little Leisure to look in it, Mr Loggan $^{134}$ having beene willing to spend some time with me to instruct me a little in Perspective, that so I may be able to send them over a Draught of my Chamber at Wieuwert when I shall be there. For any other Books I leave it to you to do as you Please, not knowing whether they will signifie any thing, or not, since I perceive that which I should be most desireous to see is not writt in a Language which I understand.

label: text
content: I was in Hopes that before this I should have had an Answeare from You to my last letter, and have received some encouragement to come into Hollond.

I will not for that Reason say to see You, But the Fine things that you told me of; Although I Hope you do beleeve that she notwithstanding is as much as ever she was

label: text
content: ## 3.1.18 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 15 January 1685; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 120-1.

label: text
content: Though you do not Chide me for not Answearing the letter I received from You Dated from Deventer $^{135}$ I cannot sattisfie my self not to Make some Apologie for it, and to let you know that my Eyes were for above a Month after so Weake that I durst not use them at all either to Write, or Read, Since when I have never beene in a Humour Good enough to Answear a Letter that so severely reprooves me for being in an Ill One. Whatever Occasion there might be for it, I durst not therefore write to you for my Life for feare of makeing some Complaints that you would have beene sure to have thought Unreasonable, as I suppose you will now think it for me to have beene so Long out of Humour, and Yet methinks Wageing War with the World, and the Flesh (as you say I do) should not seeme to you so easie a Matter but that it may very well serve to Justifie me for it. It is so long since the 8th of October $^{136}$ that I know not now what it was that I then said to you, nor what my Thoughts were. But I assure you since then, whatever you may think, I have beene much more a Stoick then you ever knew me, and have now such a Zeal for the Sect I have embraced, that I never was so sorry as since I had your letter that I am neither Handsome nor Witty; since you think such an Example would do so much Good in the World. But it is not my fault I am sure and so I indeavour to sattisfie my self, who though I am now altogether a Stoick as to my Philosophy Yet may I Hope be a Labadist too if I see it Convenient, there being no Inconsistencie I think, but a very Good Agreement betweene them. $^{137}$ Should I ever resolve for Matrimonie, You have so far improved my Reasons and Arguments for it that I should Certainly then go into

label: text
content: Freezeland, But should I do the Contrary I believe you will think it best that I stay where I am, especially since if Men should ever become my Aversion, or that I should grow extraordinarie Devout and Religious, things that sometimes Happen in that case, Here is a Friend of yours who doubts not in a little time but that she shall see her selfe an Abbess, $^{138}$ With whom I Question not but you have sufficient Interest to Procure that I may be one of Her Nuns. The Difficultie therefore lyes in makeing this Choise, and since it seems I have so far alreadie Trusted you as to Confess to You that I am but Half Armed against Matrimonie I cannot fancie that I can Pitch upon any Body better, to Advise me by which of my Halfs it is that I ought to be Determined which till you have done I meane to Converse indeed in this Present Evill world, but with such a Stoical sort of Indifference that the Brethren in Freezeland shall have no Reason to say that Damaris has forsaken them and to Convince you that there is alreadie a very great Change wrought in me I assure you I cannot remember that any discourse of Mine since I came to Towne has been able to tend at all to Mr Clarks Edification Concerning the fasions Or that Mrs Clarke and I or any other Lady have once sat in Councell about that Matter. Tis true, I am not yet got into a Tammy Petticoat $^{139}$ and Wastcoate, nor a Say Apron, $^{140}$ But the Reason is that if I should continue onely to be a Plaine Stoick I cannot yet Determine my self whether it may not be as agreable, or more so, to the Severitie of our Sect to go without any Cloaths at all, since Certainly They are a Part of, at lest Depend upon the Goods of Fortune. I Hope therefore you will be Convinced now that I am true to my Principles, and that a Proselite is not Lost, Also since My Quarrel with the World is so Lasting, that it is more likelie it was occasioned for want of a Servant, then through any falling out with any that I Had. You know I have Lived Lately a great while in a Place $^{141}$ where it has been a Complaint (as you may remember) that there was no Occasion for a Heart, and therefore the thing is not at all Unlikely. However since perhaps it may not be so much for my Honour to have it thought so, I think I am Concerned if it were but on that Score to Continue the same Here that I use to be in that Duller Aire, which for a Thousand New Reasons I was not a little glad to Quitt at this time, but should have beene much more so could I have had any Hopes of Meeting you

label: text
content: ## 3.1.19 Damaris Cudworth to John Locke, 5 June 1685; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fol. 123.

label: text
content: As Impertinent as my Letters Usually are, your last makes me think You value them so much that I am Almost Angry With my self for not haveing writt to You againe All this while and especially the Care you take of my Health seemeing to Oblige me to it, as it would have done But that I thought you could not by what I writt in my last Concerning it, beleeve my Ilness had any Danger in it, and that I could not till very lately, if I had writt, have sent you word that I was any thing better, Who was not Certainly in a more Stoical Humour when I sent my first letter to you, Then you was when you writt the first of Those that I have now by me, and Yet Perhaps at this Time I go farther then you did then, For when you Compare the World to a Dutch Inne and so on: You onely do it upon a supposition that there were no such thing as Friendship in it, But I Allowing for That, and Valueing it Perhaps as much as any Body, Can yet Beleeve it at the very Best, to be no better then an English one. Like Betty Ainsworths $^{143}$ indeed if you will, where one may be sufficiently well Treated tis true (Considering that you are yet but upon the Road) But must Pay a Most Unconscionable Reckoning for it. However methinks (for All That) wee have no Reason to Quarrel with it, since it seems to me Notwithstanding, to be very Fitt, and Just, that Things should be as They Are; and that we ought to be extreamly well Sattisfyed, and Pleased with It; as I shall be if you still After so much Absence, and Distance, Continue Your Governess in the Number of Those Few, that give you the Best Thoughts of it; who can never be less your

label: footnote
content: $^{142}$ Presumably London.

label: footnote
content: 143 Betty (Elizabeth) Ainsworth and her husband ran the notorious Rein Deer Inn in Bishop's Stortford, Hertfordshire. Prior to this, Ainsworth had been banished from Cambridge for her 'evil courses' (basically, the procuring of prostitutes). For details, see Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, edited by Robert Latham and William Matthews, 11 vols (London: HarperCollins, 1995), vol. viii, p. 466.

label: text
content: Friend then she ever was, and whom though you may easilie change for a more Deserving One, You never can for One more Sincere, and Faithfull.

label: text
content: But you will Perhaps think that I am got into a Wonderfull serious Humour, Which if your first Letter Put me In; Your last should have brought me out of; But it will not Do; Gravitie has the Ascendant I Confesse, and neither your Extraordinarie Bed, nor Hogen Mogen Gyant $^{144}$ with Dejected Whiskers, can do any more then Just make me smile: and Yet I fancie Him at Urgunda's $^{145}$ Feet as much as is Possible, who is indeed a great Diviner, and Predicter, But you Know very well that her skill is not Always Infallible. Notwithstanding I Allow that she Merits extraordinarie Homage; and I my self will Pay it Her if on the Twentie second Day of This Month, I find that she Foreknew in the Last what was to Come to Pass in my Heart. In which should she Prove in the Right (as Yet I cannot Think) That Puzling Difficultie about Matrimonie might Perhaps be soone Resolved; $^{146}$ and Your Governess (Following the Example of some other Soveraine Powers) might after a Long and Glorious Reigne Perchance Resigne Her Authoritie, and submit Her self Henceforwards to the more Humble Qualitie, and Condition, of a Subject. In which (If she should) she would not I hope Appeare to You Less Worthy of Your Esteeme at Least, then she has Hitherto had the Good Fortune to do; Since though All This, be but Fancie, without Realitie, The Bare Imagination that she would, if it were so, would be a Considerable Addition to that Uneasiness of Mind that I am in at Present Upon Diverse Accounts, which Yet Cannot hinder me (as You see) from telling you that I Constantly am

label: text
content: Your Real Friend and Servant Philoclea.
