content: for me to do otherwise. Do not Therefore I Beg of you think me Altered, Although it be true that there is no longer any Mademoiselle Cudworth in the World that I know of, Nor would your letter have found any had it come but one Half Houre later then it did, it being in the very Church that she received it, and Almost at the very same moment that she was going to quitt that name for Another Under which you will Always find her as much your Friend as she ever was, or as you can Desire that she should be.

label: text
content: I dare not say more, for Feare of Frighting you again and makeing you send for your Taylor, Although the Flatterie of your Distick $^{147}$ I confess did not at all Displeas me, being Willing to Beleeve there may be a little Truth amongst a great deal that is not so, and that you Have Assured me in Plaine Prose (which Generally is more sincere then Verse) that I still am in the number of Those who make you Prefer the World to a Dutch Inne. My Value of it, is still much at the Old Rate, As my Philosophy is still the same, However you Reproach me as not being true to my Principles; But Fortune who is more Just then you, and who Knows (it seems) How well I Merrited to be a Weiwert Sister, has on this side the Water found for me a Friend of LAbadies; so that whenever your Health Permits you to come into England You may Possibly Have as great an Inducement to bring you into Essex, $^{148}$ as I should have to see Friesland if I were with you, who if you Remember Have sometimes said that you thought Me very well Qualified to bring up a new sect; I may therefore with much more ease improve upon the Old Foundations, Do not then think that the Spirrit of Care, and Familie Affairs shall Intirely Possess me How deepe soever I may seeme to Have ingaged my self in them I am at this time Willing to Beleeve what Has beene sometimes told me, That in some sort I am Capable of any Thing that I Have either a mind to Or that it otherwise Befits me to do. However my Predominant Inclinations will I am certaine Always be the same and I shall never Help being well enough Opiniated of them Neither to oppose Them Or be Asshamed to Owne Them. The Love of my Friends Therefore and the Best Kinds of Usefull Knowledge so far as I am Capable of it, will still Possess my Heart as much as ever They did; However I deny not But that I Have had a Thousand Perplexing Imaginations of another Nature (Though not about Those Weightie Matters You Fancie) and that my Head was never so much Distracted by the Thoughts of this World, and Pittyfull Life, as it has of late beene; Nevertheless if my letter was so Grave

label: text
content: ## 3.1.21 Damaris Masham to John Locke, 15 September 1685; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 134-5.

label: text
content: Your last Letter seems to me to Differ so much from the stile of your former ones, that I cannot help being Dissattisfyed with you for it, notwithstanding the many obliging Things You have said to me in it; And you make such distinctions betweene Friendship, and Respect, Your Governess, and my Lady—that if I were at all naturally Suspicious would Incline me to beleeve you was growing Wearie of the Former. But as I am not so, I confess I cannot find either in you, Or my self, any Reason that should induce me to be of that Opinion; You having too much Judgment to be mistaken in the Choise of a Friend, and I too much Value for your Friendship to neglect Preserving it by any thing in my Power; However the Appearances, But, of Some Things, are Displeaseing; and I would not (Therefore) any more But seeme to see my self Treated by You at a Greater

However it being but the first Temptation of this Kind, in Hopes also it may be the Last, I Resolve to Prevail with my self to withstand it, Although I cannot but Hope that you Think in this Case what Mrs Phillips $^{150}$ as truely says in Another,

label: text
content: You see that I cannot yet forget my Poetry upon occasion, and I Assure you the Vehicles of the Platonists (whatever the Vortices of Des Cartes were) were Always much more my Favourites then the Muses; $^{152}$ And it is not for Guilded Coaches, and Embroidered Beds, Nor Yet the more important Considerations of a Familie, and Children, How Bountefully soever stored with Them, $^{153}$ that will with me make them give Place to those Others, There being no Inconsistencie I hope betweene being still the same Philoclea, and indeavoring to Acquitt my self as my Lady—But that is a Name which we will lay aside if you Please till you are Better Reconciled to it, and Have seene (which I cannot but Hope you once will, and that, ere very long) How Perfectly she Resembles your Governess. In the mean time Remember that in the Learned Dulness of this Place $^{154}$ there is Yet more Societie then in the Countrey And that amidst the Impertinent Wrang'lings of the Schools One may sometimes Heare something more Edifying (at least more Diverting) then in the Repeated Entertainments of the Price of Corn, and the Best Managment of a Dairie; and Consequently that I shall have more need now

content: ## (A Village less then Islington) $^{1 5 5}$

label: text
content: Who were enough to make One even in Love with a Countrey life Had he found in it afterwards, the Satisfaction he Promised Himself beforehand; But the World it seems is the same every where; and the Honest Simplicitie of the Golden Age was no more to be found at Chelsea, then in the Courts of Princes, Neither do I any more expect (though removed at something a Greater Distance from them then He) that Philoclea should find an Arcadia till the next Revolution. $^{156}$ But There are surely Better Eliziums then that was And without the Assistance of Faith I think wee may very well Hope for a more Noble Paradice then the Antediluvian One. $^{157}$

label: text
content: You see I am getting againe to the Platonists notwithstanding what you Say; Whether it be in Contradiction to you or No, I cannot tell; but to my Knowledge I never had so Great a Desire as now to Talk to you of a Vehicle; But You shall not smile upon so serious a Subject; Since I Know after All, it would but serve you for a more Ingenuous Railerie; and in the Humour I am at Present in, I should not Acquit you of Prophanation; For Know that in the Solitude of a short Widdowhood, I Have shutt my self of the World, and Retireing into my self, am Mounted as far Above it, as an Inhabitant of Clay can be; Where I look downe with Pitty on All Things Below me; and where even Witt it self seemes but an Unvaluable Bauble; Where my Ideas are too Sublime to beare the Mixture of any thing that is Material; and where the Objects of all my Thoughts are of an Immortal Nature; and such without doubt is Friendship, since I find that There; But Alass! it is of

However Reason Teaches me (for I would not have you Think that I am Mounted Above That too) to be Contented with the World as it tis, and to make the Best of every thing in it; Feare not then but that I shall Descend againe from this Pitch of Altitude; and Accept without Disdaine of such a Friendship as You can afford me.

content: But whether am I Run? And what a Pretty Answear is This to All the Complement you have sent me; But I onely Defer it; You shall stay for it till you are Newly Marryd and then I will Beg Philander to Assist me in it; who in the Meane time will I Hope Answeare All the Kind, and Sincere, Part of it, in supplying by His owne Thoughts whatever my Words have been wanting in Acknowledgment.

label: text
content: But is it not time to Conclude? Or shall I Lengthen yet this Long Letter by making an Apologie for it? In which, I have nothing to say for my self but that it is the last you are like to Have a great While; I meane not the last letter, but the last long one; Since I go very suddenly into the Countrey, where you must Allow me for some time to be more then Ordinarilie employed, Where I shall have a Great deal of Real Business, and Where if I Had none I must However seeme Busie to Acquire the Necessarie Reputation of a Good Countrey Houswife; Which should I in earnest come at length to Deserve I will Have Affidavit made of it by the most skilfull of my Neighbourhood, and send it to you to Publish for the Honour of the Muses; Who I dare say will think it no Disparagment to them; and for whose Reputation I cannot but have a Concerne since the World Here, will Beleeve me to be a Votarie of Theires whether I will, or No. But I think verylie instead of a letter I shall write a Book to You, The Title of which must I think be Miscellanies; But I will now have done; and therefore to avoid any more Impertinence, I will Conclude like other Authors,

label: text
content: Finis.

label: text
content: ## September the 15th.

label: text
content: I cannot Help improving this little Remainder of my Paper by a Postscript to let you know that I am exceeding glad of your owne Good Health and that I Know nothing lately either of Mr C[larke?]s or His Ladys. The last that I Heard of Him was that he was gone into the Countrey to her; and that he got well Thither.

label: text
content: ## 3.1.22 Damaris Masham to John Locke, 14 November 1685; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 126-7.

label: text
content: I have several times begun to write to You since I received Yours But the Necessitie of Household Affaires will have it so that I could never Yet finish one Letter; what the Fate of This will be I Know not, But I have in my designe set apart this Day to Discharge my self to my Friends of All Obligations of this Kind; In the first Rank of whom I Hope you doubt not but you stand It being Altogether impossible for any thing whatever to incroach upon the Place You have theire, whilst I may Beleeve I have any in Yours, And yet I cannot but Acknowledge that as to some Things Matrimonie and Familie Cares have Altered me very much. Though I was Always Dull, I find that I am now a Thousand times more so then formerly; And the little Knowledge that I once had, is now exchangd for Absolute Ignorance; I am taken off of All that I once did Know, and Understand; and Have nothing at All in lieu of it; Tis in Vain that you bid me Preserve my Poetry; Household Affaires are the Opium of the Soul and it is impossible for me to make use of that Preservative unless I can Recover first from this Lethargie that I am now in. Which that you may have some Hopes of However, Know that I am at Present All alone in that Place I told you of except the Gentleman you Kno of, a Young Man of 16, a Child of 5, and a Girl between both that speakes not yet a Word of English; $^{158}$ For These last you may judge what conversation They are; and for the first the Business of this World Almost wholly imploys him when he is at Home, so that I have very little of His Company. All my Friends and Relations have just left me, and the Badness of the Season Permits not now any Visits from the Neighborhood which However are not very Desireable. These things with the consideration of finding every Thing New About me may perhaps be some excuse for the Present, and afford some Hopes that when some of them are removed, and that I am Accustomed to the rest I may returne to my self againe, which I heartilie wish; since whatever Value I in my last set upon the Accomplishment of being a Countrey Housewife, I owne I slight it as much now; which is however Perhaps but the last Shift of Prudence in me who may be (as Davenant has it) What I would Prize

label: text
content: But I find I am getting into Poetry alreadie before I Have thought of it, I cannot therefore but Hope well of my self Though Certainly nothing but the Aire of Essex would have brought this Poet to my Mind. $^{160}$ That, where You are, has had a Much better effect sure upon You, though I should not have Hoped for so much from it, since how it comes about otherwise I Know not, but you are methinks of late growne a most Wonderfull Platonist Though by your leave you greatly mistake in your Accusation of the Platonique you mention, $^{161}$ if you think she has any Way Profaned those Misteries, or Degenerated from theire Principles; Souls are not fetched from those Happy Abodes, before they have forfeited Them; Nor clad in Clay, whilst they are Capable of Acting in any better Vehicle. $^{162}$ The former, is but the meanes to restore them againe to the latter, and she is so far therefore from being any way guiltie upon that score, that it is indeed the greatest Act of Platonique Charitie that she was Capable of Performing, and The Omission of it so long, the greatest thing she ought to Repent of; But it is not a yeare yet since she writt her Recantation, and Promised Amendment, (which I would now send you, since you desire Verse, but that it is too long) and she has so Honestly Kept Her Word since, that I hope she has sufficiently Merrited her Pardon for that Sin of Ignorance.

label: text
content: But how shall I do to forgive all your Abuse of me, as well as Her, Since I can neither make any Verses at this Time, nor remember any to the Purpose. But be Assured your Punishment is but Defered, since if ever that Humour come on me againe You shall Wish for Finis a Thousand times before you find it; I will set the Affronted Countrey Ladies too upon you, and They shall Abuse you Ten times more then I can, for All your Contempt of Theire Sublime Ideas of Goose Pye, and Bag Puding. $^{163}$ This would bring me again now to the Chapter of Household Affaires, and my employments; but that I am awearie; However for All my quarrel with you I cannot help telling you that there is

label: text
content: ## 3.1.23 Damaris Masham to John Locke, 14 December 1685; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 128-9.

label: text
content: It is Methinks a Long while since I writt to You and I Have not since Heard Any thing of You; Sometimes I Fancie You are not well But I more often Think that it is a Wilfull neglect of your Governess that occasions Your silence. Pardon me if I cannot Help being a little Jealous; I think you never was so long without leting me Heare from You but Once before. Methinks I still Deserve from You as much as I ever did, since I am still the same I ever was in Respect of my Friends, Unless that the loss of some of them Has made me more Covetuous of Preserving those that are left; to which you must lay the Blame of my importuning you now with Another Letter before you Have Answeared the last which as I remember was indeed

label: text
content: I Dreamt of Heareing from you last Night and I wished for it All This Day when In comes a Double letter to me just now from my Brother, $^{173}$ who never used to write to me But to inclose yours. I Began to Admire my Good Fortune extreamly; and Opened it with All the Hast imaginable expecting All the Diversion which your Letters use to Afford me, when in stead of That I find nothing But a Long Weding Compliment from a Countrey Cosen that without question has been studying for it This Half Yeare; Judge you now whether this was not a great Disappoint and Whether I can forgive You for it without makeing me a large Amends, That is, by writing me a letter Twice as Long as His without makeing any notice of Matrimonie, for I am quite sick of that subject by way of letters; and I should be very glad instead of being Wished Joy any more that you will indeavour to give me some by saying something that is more new to me. I Assure you in this Winters Solitude it will be a great Charitie, since I have not so much as the Diversion of my Dairie, and am Forced now (and Therefore I Hope it will be without Offence to the Good Housewifes of my neighborhood) to seeke my entertainment in Books Altogether; and that Principally in Poetry, to which the Present Fancie most inclines me, and Therefore know at this Time that it is out of pure Crosness that I send You none, since I Hardly write of Late to Any Body but your self in Prose. Yet do not Blame me for it, since I Have Alreadie told you that I am Jealous and it is impossible there should be any good Humour left where that Passion is. How ever perhaps you may see me in Print in a little While, and then need not be Beholden to me, it being growne much the Fasion of late for our sex, Though I confess it has not much of my Approbation because (Principally) the Mode is for one to Dye First; and at this time if I might Have my owne Choice I Have no Great Inclination That Way Though whether it be with Haveing Converst so much of late with Urgunda $^{174}$ that she has imparted any of the spirrit of Prophecie to me, or otherwise, I Know not, But I am not without some Apprehensions that I am to do so in a little Time As within Half a Yeare or There abouts, $^{175}$ which if I should out live I then Fancie I am settled in for a Pretty while However for Feare of the First let me Advise

label: text
content: ## 3.1.24 Damaris Masham to John Locke, 13 March 1686; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 132-3.

label: text
content: Had I not been Hindered by Business That Grave Impertinence $^{176}$ I should not have staid $^{177}$ for your second letter to be out of your Debt for your First, since I am Covetuous of Keeping you Always in Mine Provided you be not long in Arrears; I would have you (if I could) Always Paying, and yet Always Oweing, that so I may never be long without either the Enjoyment or Expectation of that Pleasure which yours give me; Mine that I wrote last I did Beleeve would not Come to you of a great while because I had Inclosed it in one to Mr Cl[arke?] who I thought had then beene in Towne. But understood soon after was not. However I am glad you received it at last since it has brought me so large a Returne, Nor will any more be Angry with you (though you still persist in it) either for Abuseing me, or my Neighbours, Though I must needs say after all your Railerie upon them it is in my Opinion no small Peice of Confidence in You to expect that I should find you out a Mistress amongst Them; But you do not indeed Desire it, Neither is it my Systeme of Platonisme that has Converted You; Handsome Faces, and Good Voices, afford more perswasive Arguments by much then any drawn from Philosophie, and without Them, and those Greater Charms of Witt, and Good Humour, which I doubt not Accompanie Them, I might have Preached Charitie to you long enough, and Those Distresed Souls that have Forfeited theire first Priviledges might long enough have Continued

label: text
content: in Their State of Inactivitie ere you would have had a thought of Provideing them more suitable Habitations. But why must Holland have the Honour of Converting so Obstinate a sinner as you were? Were I now in a Condition of seeing it I should Certainly for this Reason Have much Greater Curiositie to do so then ever I have yet Had, But Mine at Present (as you Know) gives me thoughts of a farther Voyage then That, and my Time of Preparation is now but short. $^{178}$ If you have any messages therefore to send, you must do it Quickly Although I confess I shall not be displeased any more then you, if after All, it should Happen that I should not go of that Errand. Nevertheless do not think that if I leave this World I do it with any Mightie Regrett, since though I could perhaps at some times have done it with less, I am yet very far from being in Love with it; I would not have you therefore Mourne for me, and on that Account, as well as another, am at a loss what Legacie to leave You, Since I have a very great Desire to leave you something. But a Haire Ring, $^{179}$ as well as Black Cloaths, might perhaps give Offence to your Dutch Mistress, and though the Dead need not much to be Feared, none who Deserve to make such extraordinarie Conquests as she has done But on such an occasion would be Jealous of Them. It would trouble my Ghost exceedingly in whatever state it finds its self, to be the Cause of any Allay to your Happiness and not to be in a Power of Justifying You in a Matter wherein it knew you to be Perfectly Innocent. But to Digress a little from so Grave a Subject Let me Know I beseech you what you meane by the Amends that you suppose you have made me in Length, Breadth, and Thickness. I have a Guess at it that makes me very Uneasie in the Want of it since Haveing not received it in All this Time I feare it is lodged in other Hands. If it be so Pray take Care to Redeeme it for me since I shall at least be so much the Better for it as to be furnishd thereby for making a more Considerable Legacie to somebody then any that I now Can, and that You may not think it will be to any unworthy of it, Know that if no Accident send me Post before the Time tis amongst the Learned, and those Particularly that you have expresed most Value for, that I intend to make my last Exit, $^{180}$ If my Part upon this Stage be indeed at an End. But this brings me before I thought of it to the Subject of Poetry, and to makeing my excuse for not Writeing in Verse, Since that Rhimeing Humour not onely went soon off But I have Almost forsworne

content: ever Leting it come on Againe, Since what was intended onely for my Owne Diversion I find has Unawares (to Use Mrs Phillips's words) exposed me to the Severitie of the Wise and the Railerie of the Witts, $^{181}$ Altho not in any Printed Volume, Or I Hope ever will, But by my owne Indiscretion in the first Place in Trusting to the Favorable Censure of my Friends, and theirs in the next in exposeing me to that of Those who were not so; $^{182}$ Nevertheless I have sent you the Paper you Desire, that You may see I will not make any excuses to You, Although how far it is Pertinent to the Subject we were Upon I cannot tell, since it was writt some Months before ever I saw Sir Francis Neither can I tell now how I came to Mention it Unless for being reproached with it that very Day I Hapned to write to You which I well remember I was I have shortned it what I could, by Leaveing out the Begining, more Impertinent then the Rest, the Person it is Addresed to Haveing as little share in it as Usually Friends in the Countrey Have, serveing in Reallitie but for Pretence. Whether any other Had more, or No, is not I think Material to Say, But if they Had, I Beleeve 'twill be Needless to tell you it was not any Philosopher of the Platonic Sect. I Hope now that I shall have Appeased You, and that You will for once give me Fritters, for my Fritters, $^{183}$ and let me have Both the French Sonnet, and Your Translation. It is late, and I have writt till I am so sleepie I scarse Know what I say, I shall therefore onely Add the Returne of my Thanks to Philander for All the Good Wishes I had sent me at the Begining of the Yeare by Paul Hobson. $^{184}$ Pray Assure him that I wish Him All the same and more if it be Possible and that I am with as much Friendship as His Faire Platonick will give me leave

content: an Errant Gossip to be Gadding $^{194}$ Abroad so soone Againe, And but an Ill Wife when I tell you that I have left my Good Man at Home alone by Himself, But the Little Being $^{195}$ I mentioned in my Last must be my Excuse for it, and I doubt not will seeme a Sufficient one since you have thought fitt to send me a Postscript of Consolation for being but at Thirtie Miles Distance, But I gave I Question not a Just Occasion for it, which though it proceeded from a Cause I cannot Alter, your Letter has I Confess made me a little Asshamed of. But leaveing This subject Let me tell you that I am much Pleased with the Preference you have given me over your Dutch Mistress; and that You can Think that Friendship may have the Ascendant over Love; I am Pleased Because it is Natural to All to Desire that Those whom they Esteeme should have the same Opinions with Themselves, were it onelie out of a Just Value for Truth; But I am more so (I was going to say) for a more Obliging Reason; But that I have Recalled to my Remembrance You might Possibly not be in Earnest; and if so, that it would be in Vaine to Perswade you into it (without which it must lose its Value) especially under the Disadvantages of my owne Absence, and your Misstreses Presence; And indeed should I attempt it now I think of That, it would more Argue my Little Opinion of the Latter, then my Great One of the Former. For what Signifies an Absent Friend? One sees them not; One Converses not with Them, but by the Tedious way of Letters; And one has never with any Freedome the most Proper and Pleaseing Sattisfactions of Friendship, To Laugh with Them when one is Merry; And to Complaine to them when one is Sad; So that to Confess the Truth to you, Though I have now a Friend with me Less Agreable then you Are (As perhaps your Dutch Mistress may in some Respect or other be then me) I enjoy much more Pleasure from them then I should in You (were you Capable of having an Equall Regard for me) at This Distance. And yet after All, Haveing said this more to Justifie You then for any thing else (Although it is not without much Truth) I am yet Pleased that you Remember me, That you Desire to Heare from me, And that you think I write not often enough to You. And to let you Know that if you had as Deserving a Friend, nothing could make them Altogether Useless and Insignificant, Philander is a Name, that since I have seene you, has many times Reconciled me to the World when nothing else would; When I have beene in This Place Plagued with Theire Pedantry

content: and scholastick Arrogance; $^{196}$ when in Towne with the Noisie Fops $^{197}$ There; And when with the Insipid Coxcombs $^{198}$ of the Countrey; But Above All I have made use of it (though whether with so much Reason, or No, You and Heaven Can Onely Tell) when I Have beene Tempted to Beleeve that there was no such Thing Below (amongst your Sex at least) as an Undesigning and Honest Friendship; free from Unjust Ends; and Little Interests; which when either Disappointed; or Served; turns to Hatred, Malice, and Revenge; Or to Coldness, and Indifference; Were I satisfyed that you ever had any Real Friendship for your Governess I should be Abundantly so that I was in the Right in Reflecting upon it to This End, and on These Occasions, But the Doubt Lies on That Side; and I Dare not Determine with Assureance whether I ever was more to you then an Agreable Acquaintance. But I know not whether I Have Rambled; from the Text I am Certaine, though what you writt to me I cannot well tell, Haveing lost your Letter, A Misfortune which never before Befell me, as well as the Receiving it Open, which I wonder at. Twoo things notwithstanding I Remember in it The One that you chid me for not writeing sooner; The other that you was Angry with me for not Dyeing; For the first, my Apprehensions of the last was the Principle Reason of it; Since I envyed any Body but my self the Pleasure of Reading a Letter of yours. And for the Last I Have no excuse to make for spoiling a good Epitaph; But can Assure you that I was so far a Prophetess as to be in very great likelihood of it; My Long Weakness after which, is Another excuse for my Former Fault, Who whether I write to You or No shall Always be Your Real Friend

content: notwithstanding the Postscript I should not have beene well Pleased with it, but have looked on you as one who wanted Sensibilitie for the Afflictions of your Friends; Yet being now able to Judge without Any Prepossession I must acknowledge that I do not think I should have had much Reason for it; That you should therefore have been so Uneasie upon that Score is extreamly Obliging and is no small Argument of the Realitie of that Friendship you Profess, Which if I did Doubt of, The Rareness of it in the World, And my want of Merrit to have Deserved it from you, may I think be Grounds Sufficient for my Excuse; Although I do not Apprehend that this Cartesian Principle $^{200}$ ought at All to have offended you, the End sufficiently Justifying the use of it. Upbraid me not Therefore with what I owe you; Ingratitude is a Thing not in my Nature and I believe without Vanitie I may say it none better understands then my self the Value of a Sincere Friendship. For the Preference you Pretend to give me over your Dutch Mistress, You must Pardon me if not being willing to Question the Truth of what you say I beleeve notwithstanding what you tell me of her Merrit (which you Dare Compare, and I doubt not Justly enough May, with Anie in my Neighborhood) Tis yet more to some Defect in That, then to the Greatness of my Owne, Or Any thing else, that I am Indebted; It being Hard else to Conceive that Friendship should be Able to make its Party Good against Love under so Unequal a Disadvantage as Absence. Think not that I would lessen the Obligation I have to You (If you Apprehend no Hazard of making me a Desperate Debtor I Know not why I should) But Friendship will have an Advantage not Inconsiderable if she should onelie Triumph over Beautie and Kindness; The first you have told me your Mistress has in a Verie Eminent Degree And the Last I have much Reason to Beleeve. It cannot Therefore be a Conquest too Little for me Although she may not deserve to make you Hers; which Yet Perhaps you may be more then you your self are Aware, For I cannot Conceive how it is Possible (especially in a Countrey where Agreable Women are but Scarse) that she should Hang Long in that Strange Posture you speake of; If she dos, I am Confident the Fault must be Hers, and I have no disposition to blame you for it; A Mistress is the most Dangerous thing in the World to a Friend, and Therefore she must Pardon me if I cannot be verie much Hers, as I hope you will do too if I speak not of Her with All that Respect which from One Unprejudiced against her may yet perhaps be her Due, For in spight of what you tell me of my worst Letters

content: giveing you more Pleasure then she Can in Her Best Humour Tis verie Hard for me to beleeve so well either of my self, or your Preference of Friendship, when I Reflect on a Great Beautie on the One Side, And Yeares of Absence on the Other. However tis no small satisfaction that I can stand my Ground, And the Obligation I have to you is not a little that whatever others have gained, I am no Loser; Since methinks Besides your telling me so, I find several Reasons to Perswade me I am still to you the same Person that I was when you could Indure to Pass so many Hours in my Companie; at least that I should be so, if your Health would permit you to see me in that Place you Pretend so much Curiositie for; For I cannot find but that our Opinions of Absence after All are much the same, since you have no Reason from my last or any Thing else to Beleeve my Esteeme for my Friends can be Lessend by it; And in your Confessing it a Misfortune, you your self Acknowledge the Pleasure of Haveing Them <Is>, Since else it Could be no Misfortune. Could you find an Expedient to make it less so I should have a great Obligation to you for it But I can think of none, unless instead of Letters, you should write me Volumes. I Thought a good while since you had sent me One you writt Long Ago But I perceived afterwards it was a Mistake. If Anie such thing were made Publick (though I am now out of the Land of Philosophy) I suppose I should some way or other have known it But something that I had before heard at London gave me Occasion to Misunderstand you and Also to Put me in Paine on that Score for my Friends the Platonists and Cartesians On whose Accounts we have formerly had so manie Quarrels. $^{201}$ But you will Perhaps, think now tis no longer Pardonable for me (If ever it were so) to Talk of Subjects of That Nature, and that Culpepper $^{202}$ and the Countess of Kents Receits $^{203}$ afford more Suitable Speculations for a Countrey Lady who has Children and a Familie to look after. Yet if you do, whilst you allow me so large a Share in Your Esteeme, and are so well satisfyed the World should Know that you Do So, I shall neither Quarrel with you for it, Or think I want Sufficient Reason to Value my Self; That, Haveing I assure you Always been a

content: ## 3.1.27 Damaris Masham to John Locke, 17 January 1687; in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, Locke MS c.17, fols. 140-1.

label: text
content: Whether or no it be longer then Ordinarie since I heard from you I cannot tell But it seems to me a great while; I am in a Humour at Present that would not give me so much satisfaction in Any thing as in the Assurance of the Remembrance of some for whom I have no Common Esteeme. And the next Pleasure that I can find to That is to let Them see that they have mine. You must Pardon therefore to that Cause the Interruption that this may give you from some better employment then the Reading my Impertinences My Letters are Always such at the Best but I have Reason to think that this will be more then ordinarilie so since the Spirrit which Dictates it is a very Unreasonable One. I am at a loss Alreadie to Know what to Say and yet I cannot Perswade my self to give over the designe of Writeing you a Letter To what Purpose should you know that I am in an Ill Humor (since in short that is the thing which I would tell you) when perhaps before This comes to you I may be Returned to a good One Or if I be not tis not in your Power to help it? Yet Could I certainlie tell as what Moment you received This it would at that verie time I fancie, bring your Idea so livelie into my Mind when you were wont to Chide me out of Vaine troubles that I verylie think it would have almost the same effect as if you your self were Present But this Cannot be and therefore I must be Content to waite till a Better Temper dos of its self or assisted by some other Happy Accident take Place and Dispell those Clouds of Melancholy that Represent everie thing either as Sad and Displeaseing, or at best Emptie and Insipid; and Onelie serve to Obscure the Light of Reason, and All good Understanding.

label: text
content: Were I ever Capable of Philosophizing I believe I might find some Solid Argument now against Materialists since I clearlie perceive in my self that a Disturbed Mind and Disordered Body such as will not permit the free Exercise of Reason in Any thing else besides, dos the more Indispose to those Spirritual Speculations which sometimes so well serve to beare up the Mind in such a due degree of Tranquilitie as is necessarie Both to the Injoyment of Life and performing the Duties of it as one ought. content: not Allow of This whatever I thought; for that Reason therefore I shall not Attempt it, though I assure you I am in so Dull and Earthy a Dispensation $^{204}$ at This time that I am not Capable of Any Discourse of Reason upon anie subject whatsoever Neither do I now Know whether I express what I would say so as to be Intelligible But you have had this Complaint so often from me that I ought to feare wearying you with it, and I should do so did I not think you would believe I would not make it so often were not the very Complaining its self some releife to the Humor that Causes it, and then I cannot doubt but you will have the Charitie to allow of it. Besides it springing more from Internal then External Causes I should be Asshamed to Discover so much Folly to One that were less my Friend; Not that I esteeme not your Opinion of me more then most Peoples But you better Kno then They how to Value what is Well, and to make Allowances for what is not so. I must therefore tell you How Unreasonable I am; I Fancie sometimes our World Here is Alterd from what it was But I think againe that That is but a Foolish Thought and that I being more Concerned in it the longer I live may think so onelie for that Reason. Otherwise there surely Always was Abundance of Malicious Ungratefull Censorious People and indeed very few besides; Could you teach me how to regard them no more then so many little Angry Wasps I should have a great obligation to you and methinks it is but a Reasonable Peice of Pride that I should do so; I Beleeve[?] I want it not in other things since Besides All This a Thing that is really the most Uneasie to me Almost of Anie thing else, Is, that there are so very Few People that I can Possibly have Any High Esteeme for; Not but that since I have seene you I have had the good fortune to be Knowne to Diverse Whom All the World that can Judge, speake of with Honour, and I have been Obliged to them for some Particular marks of Respect and Good Will; But at Present I am onelie Capable of takeing my measures from a Countrey Conversation since the rest is like to signifie very little to me; I am Certainlie Placed in the Wretchedest Neighborhood in the whole World and never had so Violent a Desire in my life as now to good Companie. Tis in Vaine that I think (and therefore Pray say nothing of it) of Suiting my Mind to my Condition, for Business and the Impertinent Concernes of a Mistress of a Familie will never have Anie Place in my Heart, and I can at most do no more then submit to Them. I wish I could do otherwise with All my Heart but tis in Vaine to strive against the streame. You will perhaps Advise me to Converse with the Dead since Here are so few Liveing

label: text
content: Though I never was more excuseable for not Writeing then at this time Yet I the least Know how to Justifie my self to you on that Score, to whom I am so much Indebted; But I Hope my Credit is good enough with You to have my Word taken; who without doubt think of my Friends much oftner the[n] I tell them so, Which I should not indeed now Do, Though you have beene in my Thoughts everie day this long while, did I not feare you might otherwise suspect the Truth of it, and that I think my self likewise indispensably Obliged to it by the Rules of Civilitie; Else (besides the disorder, and Confusion, that one may be supposed to find in a Familie so Numerous as mine, after Halfe a Yeares Absence) The Parting with a Father, Mother, and Child, besides other Friends, and returning to such a Solitarie Wilderness as This is, Puts one unavoidably into so Dull a Humour that tis impossible to Think one should be Capable of Diverting either Ones self, or Others; And indeed Could you see me at this time I am Confident That you would be Convinced that I am as arrant a Countrey Lady as any Between This and St Michaels Mount. $^{205}$ So That indeed How much soever I owe for it, I should defer my Thanks for

content: the Care you take of my Health which I thank God I now enjoy verie well, till Another time; Did not my Desire to returne Them you for Acquainting me with your little French Man $^{206}$ prevail with me to Send them Both together; I was at a loss at first by the Discription you made of Him, to guess whether he were some Poore Protestant, Or Disbanded Officer However when he Came I was so Dull I assure you, as to Converse with Him above an Houre without makeing Any Reflection On His Liverie So that without being beholden to That Recommendation You gave Him He found for His owne Sake as Favourable a reception as it is Possible He should find from one so Orthodox as my self; Who am Perfectly Agreed with Him in the Thing for which He Contends; And fancie He speakes so much Reason for it as it is Impossible that Any should Answere. However if I may enter farther into His Opinions, I am Confident He has some that He cannot maintain without Wresting the Text as much to serve His Turne as any others Can do to serve Theirs However (if I had not a Suspicion that He was an Old Friend of Mine) I would yet by no Meanes have Him Branded with the Name of a Heretick, since If the Will be Necessarilie Concerned in That, I see not the Reason for it As also that it is what may be returned by everie Partie Who I suppose All imagine Themselves in the Right. I Confess for my owne Part I do And Think my Author as much in the Wrong in That matter as any one can But I Hope that will be so far from lessening His Good Thoughts of me that it will rather increase them, since I am so Intirely (as to the rest) of His mind; and so very truely

label: footnote
content: 206 It is not clear who (or what) 'your little French Man' refers to. It is possible that this is a reference back to Masham's letter of 3 October 1687 (not included in the present volume), in which Masham notes that she has recently read an anonymous book titled Commentaire philosophique and says, 'I have a Strong fancie that it is a French Man and being much in Love with the Author wish it may be some friend of yours' (Correspondence of John Locke, vol. iii, p. 278). This book is the famous tolerationist work of the French sceptic Pierre Bayle (1647-1706), published in Amsterdam in 1686. It is possible that Locke sent her an additional copy of Bayle's Commentaire, since her comments about 'Wresting the Text' accord with this work: it offers a reading of Christ's words in the Gospel of Luke (14:23). Of course, it is also possible that here Masham refers to a work by Locke himself, such as his Epitome (Abrégé); her next letter (3.1.29) is a critique of that work, an abridgement of his Essay in French. But Locke did not send copies of the Abrégé to England till 28 February 1688 (see Correspondence of John Locke, vol. iii, pp. 388-9).

label: text
content: Though a Varietie of Accidents $^{208}$ such as are Incident to one who has so many Relations and Interests in This World dos at this time more then Ordinarilie Disorder my Thoughts, that I have not that Command of them I could Wish Yet I cannot resolve to let you think as you say if I Writt not soone you should, That the Book you did me the favor to send me, for which I returne you many Thanks, is Condemned to the Prophan Side (as you Call it) of my Closet. You are indeed in the Right to Beleeve That I do not Practice all the Rules of the Neighborhood; And that my Kitchen and Dairie, do not ingross All my Time. But how much you were so, if you Thought me Any Judge of the Essay $^{209}$ you sent me when I shall tell you I have made very little Improvment of that Kind, it will be needless to Say; I do not I confess think my self altogether Uncapable of Things of that Nature; And I am sure I have a Universal Love for All usefull Knowledge Beyond that Capacitie; But as I was Diverted from It when I was Young, first by the Commands of Others And Afterwards by that Weakness which Hapned in my Sight, The World through long Acquaintance begun almost to Claime All my Thoughts; And from my many Concerns now in It, Thinks to Justifie that Title; But as it is a True Bondage in my esteeme; and a very Ignoble One too; I assure you it is my Principle Care and Business to Free my self from It; But for one so much Ingaged, and whose Time is so far spent, the Shorter Methods are Certainly the Best: Besides that being my self Cured of some sort of Scepticisme by arguments that However Solid in them selves have beene to me effectual, I think that I may much more Advantageously employ my Houres in Pursuing the End $^{210}$ of these speculations then in indeavouring to Extricate those Difficulties that the Witts of Men have Intangled them with, Which being Needless to my self, can be no Part of my Obligations; who should not be likely to be in any Capacitie of Dispensing to Others: The Duty Certainly

Religion is the Concernment of All Mankind; Philosophy as distinguished from It, onely of Those that have a freedome from the Affaires of the World; Which as They would Hinder the latter; May well Managed be Great Inforcements of the Former: And indeed the Pleasures of This life are so Triffling and Transitorie, And Its Cares so many and Bitter, That I think one must be very Miserable and Stupid, not to seeke Ones satisfaction in some thing else; If one beleeves that it is to be found; especially as the Conjuncture $^{211}$ of some Certaine Times may Be; Which may stir up a more then ordinarie Desire of being of so Confirmed and Settled a Judgment as should secure one from the Danger of foregoing Solid and Real Goods for Imaginarie; Or on the Other Side indureing Real Inconvenience for meere Humour, and Opinion: Which I Beleeve will afford as little Satisfaction Hereafter, as Here. I Know not what Thoughts this will make you Have of me; But I suppose none of Them will be That I intend to set up a Lecture of Divinitie, Or Enter into All the Disputes and Differences of Religion; Since I belieeve to Know whatever Truth I am Concerned in is; an Easier and Better Way to Overlook $^{212}$ them; But I tell you This, to let you see that in All this time the Spirrit of Government dos not yet so Possess me but that I am as readie to give an Account of my self as receive one of my Charge; Though Principally indeed it be to Answr That Part of your Letter in which you say It will become me to show you your Mistakes: I confess I have a Desire to Know them my self (Because Yours) if there be Any; And Accordingly as opportunitie Serves, shall employ better Judgment then my owne to find them out; which if to me unanswerable, You will give me leave I Know to Propose them from a second Hand. For my owne Part though I think of several things Confusedly that I would say to you if you were in this Closet, I find them not well enough Deliberated to send so far: Though I should be glad more Clearely and fully to understand the Difference betweene you and some Friends of Mine, about that Principle thing, of the Souls Haveing no Actual Knowledge; $^{213}$ Being not sure the Difference betweene You, is Really so great as it Seemes; $^{214}$ Since

label: footnote
content: the Epitome Locke claims that the mind is 'void of all innate characters' which might have put Masham in mind of More's claim that knowledge is not written in the mind like astronomical characters. For a transcription of the Epitome in English, see John Locke, Abstract of the Essay'in The Life and Letters of John Locke, edited by Lord King (London: Bell & Daldy, 1864), pp.365-99 (p.366).

label: footnote
content: 215 This entire sentence is taken almost verbatim from Henry More's Antidote Against Atheism: 'when I say actuall Knowledge, I do not mean that there is a certain number of Ideas flaring and shining to the Animadversive Faculty, like so many Torches or Starres in the Firmament to our outward sight, or that there are any Figures that take their distinct places, and are legibly writ there like the Red letters or Astronomical Characters in an Almanack: but I understand thereby an active sagacity in the Soul, or quick recollection, as it were, whereby some small businesses being hinted unto her, she runs out presently into a more clear and larger conception. . . Suppose a skilfull Musician fallen asleep in the field upon the grasse... [his friend] jogs him and awakes him, and desires him to sing this or the other Song, telling him two or three words of the beginning of the Song, whereupon he presently takes it out of his mouth, and sings the whole song' (More, Collection, p. 17). Margaret Cavendish also comments on this passage (see 1.3.6 in this present volume).

label: footnote
content: 216 Here Masham refers to ideas about sensible qualities that are common to a number of seventeenth-century figures. In his Epitome, Locke himself mentions the examples of 'red and blue, sweet and bitter', and 'warmth, hunger, blueness or sweetness' (Locke, 'Abstract of the Essay', pp. 366, 369). On the ancient atomist views, see Ralph Cudworth, The True Intellectual System of the Universe: The First Part; Wherein, All the Reason and Philosophy of Atheism is Confuted; And Its Impossibility Demonstrated (London: Richard Royston, 1678), pp. 28-9, 47-9.

content: fitter Humour for It then Any I have beene in since I received your Book, are not much Inclined now to dwell long on these Matters; Haveing onely regard to them so far as they may Weaken, or establish in the Minds of Any the foundations of Natural or Revealed Religion; I am not therefore Dissatisfyed that Men (even those I most Esteeme) differ in these things as well as others Whilst They Agree in Those: And though (so far as I can Judge) I do Think the Demonstration of a God from His Idea Conclusive, $^{218}$ Yet were there no Other but yours, $^{219}$ I should think it sufficient. Though I can scarse think the Idea of Eternitie should be Formed from That of Time repeated; Since no Succession but must once have beene all of it to Come but one moment; And there is no Imagining (I think) an Eternal Succession. But it is surely from what you say in that last Place, That nothing could ever have Come from Nothing; $^{220}$ Or Any thing ever have beene if there once was nothing; From whence, One Cannot but Imagine the Necessarie Existence of Something; which is the same thing with Eternal Duration; which is not Properly, but onely Applicatively Successive; Containing in it Virtually all Successive Duration as the Channel of a River is always Present to the Water that Passes through it; or a Permanent Rock to the River that runs by it. $^{221}$ For the three last Things about Revelation $^{222}$ I fancie I need not say that I am so far of your

label: footnote
content: 218 Masham possibly alludes to Descartes's ontological argument in his Meditations, based on his idea of God as an infinitely perfect being. In his Antidote Against Atheism, Henry More develops and defends this Cartesian proof. For details of More's argument for the necessary existence of God, see 2.1.1 in this volume.

label: footnote
content: 219 In his Essay, Locke shuns those arguments that depend upon an idea of God in favour of a causal proof that depends on knowledge of his own existence (see Locke, Essay IV.x.1-19). The Abrégé includes the first six sections of Locke's chapter on the existence of God.

label: footnote
content: 220 Locke's arguments for the existence of God frequently appeal to the principle ex nihilo nihil fit ('nothing comes from nothing'). At the end of Essay IV.x.11, for example, Locke says that it is as impossible that non-thinking matter should produce a thinking thing, as that nothing should produce something (Essay IV.x.11). In her Discourse, Masham presents a proof for God based on a similar principle: 'I suppose it must be replyed by such a one, That as he was not the Author of his own Being, and saw clearly that he could not be produced by nothing; He was thereby led to the Acknowledgment of a Superiour Being, to whom he was indebted for his own; and therefore stood obliged to love him' (Discourse, pp. 62-3).

label: footnote
content: 221 Masham echoes More's observation in the Divine Dialogues, that it is 'not harder to conceive how Continuity of Duration is also compatible to the Divine Existence, as well as Eternity or Life eternal, which comprehends the Idea's of all Things and Ages at once in the Intellect of God. For it is . . . like the Permanency of a steady Rock by which a River slides; the standing of the Rock as well as the sliding of the River, has a Continuity of Duration'; Henry More, Divine Dialogues, Containing sundry Disquisitions & Instructions (London: James Flesher, 1668), pp. 60-1. For a similar analogy, see Cudworth, True Intellectual System, p. 645.

label: text
content: I suppose you have before this time received a letter from me by the Young Man I told you of; $^{223}$ Who I Hope is now well againe, But I Heare upon his going over was very ill with a Flux which He feared would bring Him into a Consumption; The Account came from Himself else we should have beene more Concerned; However though He I think would make the Worst of it, It would be a Satisfaction to me to be assured He is in no such Danger, Since he is one I should be very loath to lose though I have so many. Pray if he ever continue neare you to be so Kind as to give Him Any Council you may see Him to Stand in need of; He has so much good Nature and Sence That I am sure He will take It as he ought And you will therein very much Oblige me; who though I know no Ill or Extravagance by Him, Cannot but Apprehend so Young a Man left wholly to his Owne Government may easilie be drawne into Any. I have a great deal of Concerne for Him on many Accounts But all are not fit to be put in a letter. If he has not yet beene with you I am Confident it is that he has not beene well enough to leave the Hague; which I should be sorry to Think. Pray when you write to me do me the favor to let me know if He has recovered all ill effects of His distemper though I expect to Heare from him before that time. Pardon this Addition to the rest I beseech you and beleve me always your faithfull Friend and Servant

label: text
content: ## 3.2 Damaris Cudworth Masham and Jean Le Clerc

label: text
content: Jean Le Clerc was a Genevan Protestant and the editor of three influential periodicals: Bibliothèque universelle et historique (1686-93), Bibliothèque choisie (1703-13), and Bibliothèque ancienne et moderne (1714-27). It seems likely that Masham became acquainted with Le Clerc through Locke the two men were friends in Amsterdam during Locke's period of exile in Holland, and a few years prior to the correspondence selected here Le Clerc had written to Masham at Oates, to send her a book. But it is also possible that Masham was introduced to Le Clerc independently of Locke-she was a correspondent of Le Clerc's good friend Philippus van Limborch, a professor of Remonstrant theology in Amsterdam, and Limborch had previously been in correspondence with Masham's father, Ralph Cudworth, and his colleague Henry More. $^{224}$

label: text
content: ## 3.2.1 Damaris Masham to Jean Le Clerc, 18 June 1703; in the Special Collections of the University of Amsterdam, Ms. J 58.

label: text
content: Oates 18 June 1703.

label: text

That I writt not to you on that occasion my self was truely onelie from a Scruple that I made of [not] wasting Time that is always so usefully employed as yours is: and I could not know that you complained of want of leisure wherein to write to Mr Locke, $^{228}$ and think it fit to impose the reading of my letters upon you; which, Perhaps, also, your great Civilitie might either have ingaged you to answer, or have made you uneasie in not doing so: and I had not the Vanitie to think that my Approbation, or Admiration, mingled, possibly, with some little trifling, or inconsiderable objections that I might then have to make, were material enough to give you such trouble. What I could with most satisfaction have told you would have beene what I before had desired you to Beleeve, and what with Pleasure I repeat, that is, That I have a very great Esteeme for You, which I should be glad to express by any Real service, were I capable of doing so. You should receive letters from me on such an occasion everie Post; however the weakness of my Eyes Comply with your want of leisure to make me decline writing on subjects barely of Civilitie, or Ceremonie: for they are not strong enough to hold out well for all the use I have, or would Willingly make of them: although they never were in any either Apparant, or Invisible Likelihood, that I know of, of leaving me in the Dark; as Mr Norris long ago perswaded many that they had done, by a Printed Letter to me to Console me for being Blind. $^{229}$ I know not whether before this comes to your Hands you will have received Dr Bulls Works $^{230}$ from me, or No; but finding that you had mentioned him in yours Ars Critica $^{231}$ as an Author that you esteemed,

content: I am much obliged by the favour of your letter, and owe you great acknowledgments for the Books you have sent me, wherein I find not onely instruction, and entertainment, but Particular obligation. No one can have more respect for the memorie of a Dead Parent or Friend than I have for my Fathers; and it is no little satisfaction to me to see that a work of his, thought excellent by the best Judges of such a Performance, will be by your means more knowne in the World than it has hitherto been. The Book now Begins to grow rare; and I hope it may within a few years receive another impression. One cause of its having been less looked after (as Mr Churchil $^{234}$ tells me) has been its being apprehended to be but an imperfect work; which though it indeed was in respect of the Authors designe: Yet considered as a discourse against Atheisme, it is Compleat. $^{235}$ You was told truely that a Second Part to this was left by the Author: which Second Part yet was both first in his intention, and also first writt by him: what concerned the Atheistick Fate being

label: footnote

content: 235 The title page of Cudworth's True Intellectual System describes the work as 'The First Part; Wherein All the Reason and Philosophy of Atheism is Confuted; And Its Impossibility Demonstrated'. In the preface, Cudworth then tells his readers that he intends to publish two more parts to the work. The other two parts would demonstrate, first, that there is a 'Natural, Eternal, and Immutable Justice, or Morality'; and, second, that 'we have some Liberty, or Power over our own Actions' (True Intellectual System, 'Preface', sig. $ ^{*} r ). These works never appeared in his lifetime. The first part was published posthumously as the Treatise concerning Eternal and Immutable Morality in 1731; and the second was published as A Treatise of Freewill in 1838. Additional manuscripts on free will by Cudworth can be found in the British Library, London, Add. MSS 4978-82.

That this second Part is yet in Being, I believe; though had the Will of the Dead been performed it had not long survived its Author. Nor was his Injunction to this Purpose from a sudden or late resolution, but a Determination which I remember to have heard him often speak of when I was a Girl, though not with an intention of neglecting what he had designed, but of writeing anew upon the same matter as not thoroughly satisfied with what he had writ: which still remains, I suppose, in the hands of my Brother; $^{236}$ whose intentions concerning it are wholly unknown to me. That which made my Father delay so long the Prosecution of what he intended was Partly that obstruction which an uncertaine Health gave to his Studies; and partly his being ingaged accidentally in other Designs, which were unhappily likewise left unfinished. I am much obliged by the regard you express for the Honour of a Person who was once so Deare to me: and what you Contribute to his Reputation in the World ingages me to be always from a Just acknowledgment, no less than I have long been from a great esteeme, very truely your servant.

content: Doctors, who quarrel one with another upon this Controversie in theire Learned writeings, $^{240}$ instruct us (Out of the Pulpit) onely to hold fast the Form of Sound words: and tell us but what we should Not Beleeve; not what we should Beleeve, in a Matter on which (whatever they think in regard of themselves) I, from hence Hope they are perswaded that Our Salvation does not depend. Such as I am, being thus safe in Ignorance, whilst they can no sooner explicitely Beleeve, than they become Heterodox on one side, or other, We should (I think) be in the right not to Perplex our selves with this Question, had we not yet a better Reason for not doing so, from the silence of the Scriptures herein. To distinguish Nominal Trinitarianisme from Socinianisme; and Real Trinitarianisme from Tritheisme; $^{241}$ and to Decide which of these Opinions is best supported by Antiquitie are matters for you Learned and Knowing Men: I cannot yet but wish that such as your Self might always employ theire Labours upon things of the most Profitable and universal use. May God grant you long life and Health to be further this way Beneficial to the World: and may you always enjoy such Happyness as may make you think long life a Blessing to your Self. I am

The Systematical Men will hardly I doubt be able to answer him thorowly, but especially the Calvinistical; in whose Orthodoxie he is so intrenched, that those Divines can scarce have one faire Blow at him. And it is really sad to see that whilst such Teachers of the People do with so cruel heat (as they too often do) fall upon some men onely for dissenting from them in Opinions which are no Doctrines of Christianitie; and represent for dangerous Heretics such (for example) as You are; they at the same time are forced patiently to hear Religion ridiculed without dareing to oppose the man who dos it, from a Feare (but too Just) that they should thereby afford him matter of greater Triumph. label: text
content: ## 3.3.1 Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz to Damaris Masham [early 1704?]; in Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Bibliothek: Niedersächsische Landesbibliothek zu Hannover, LBr. 612, fols. 1-2.

label: text
content: I have been informed that you are sending me a copy of the Intellectual System of the late Mr Cudworth. There is hardly an honour that could touch me more deeply, with respect to the person who grants it, and at the present time. I first saw this book in Rome, where the highly reputed French Mathematician Mr Auzout $^{251}$ had brought it with him, and it was a delight to see the finest thoughts of antiquity's sages put into context, and accompanied by sound reflection: in a word, great erudition and equal insight, joined together. The subject also interests me greatly, as I have thought long and hard about it. I would even claim to have discovered a new country in this intelligible world, and to have thereby added a little to this great system that your father has left us, Madam, after having it pass through the hands of the best ancient and modern thinkers, and then enriched by his own. My addition consists, amongst other things, of a small system of pre-established harmony among substances, $^{252}$ of which Mr Bayle speaks amply in both editions of his wonderful dictionary, $^{253}$ in the Rorarius article $^{254}$ but even more in the

label: footnote
content: 250 This letter and all subsequent letters from Leibniz to Masham have been translated from the French. Because nearly all the surviving Leibniz manuscripts are rough drafts, I have chosen not to annotate the multiple amendments and deletions in those drafts, to make the letters as accessible and comprehensible to readers as possible. I am extremely grateful to Jillian Britton and Alexei Procyshyn for their assistance with these translations.

label: footnote
content: 251 Adrien Auzout (1622-91), now best-known as an astronomer. Leibniz visited Rome in the spring of 1689.

label: footnote
content: 252 Leibniz's metaphysical theory of pre-established harmony is the theory that the soul is created such that everything in it arises from its own internal nature, in perfect accordance or conformity to the things outside it.

label: footnote
content: 253 Pierre Bayle was the author of the Dictionnaire historique et critique [Historical and Critical Dictionary], a vast encyclopedia of historical figures and places, first published in French in 1697, with a revised and expanded second edition in 1702. For a modern selection of entries in English, see Pierre Bayle, Historical and Critical Dictionary: Selections, translated and edited by Richard H. Popkin, with the assistance of Craig Brush (Indianapolis, IN: Bobbs-Merrill, 1965).

Bayle then provides an analysis of the shortcomings of the Aristotelian theory of animal souls, on the one hand, and the Cartesian doctrine of the beast machine, on the other. Referring to Leibniz as 'one of the greatest minds in Europe' Bayle suggests that Leibniz's philosophy might dispel some of the difficulties raised by animal ingenuity (Bayle, Dictionary, p. 218). For an English translation of Bayle's Remarks H and L, and Leibniz's replies, see Leibniz's 'New System' and Associated Contemporary Texts, translated and edited by R. S. content: Pleasure any occasion of testifying a great respect for you, and has lately suggested to me that my Fathers Intellectual System might, possibly, not be unacceptable to you. The esteem you express for that work pleases me very much both on this account, and also as it is a new Confirmation to me of the Worth of that Performance.

label: text
content: I should be glad to have a farther view into the Intellectual World; and would therefore willingly have right conceptions of the system you propose. $^{256}$ To this purpose upon the receipt of your obliging Letter, I looked into the Article of Rorarius in the first Edition of Mr Bayls Dictionarie (not having the second by me) and being by his quotation of you there, directed to the Journal des Savans 1695, $^{257}$ I read what is there published of it. Perhaps my not being accustomed to such abstract Speculations made me not well comprehend what you say there of Formes, upon which I think you build your Hypothesis: for (as it seems to me) you sometimes call them Forces Primitives, $^{258}$ sometimes des Ames, $^{259}$ sometimes Formes constitutives des substances, $^{260}$ and sometimes substances themselves; but such yet as are neither Spirit, nor Matter, whence I confess I have no cleare Idea of what you call Formes.

label: text
content: That a man whose correspondence is so highly esteemed as yours by all the Learned Men of Europe should employ any of his valuable moments <in the> instruction <of an> Ignorant Woman is what I should not perhaps presume to importune you for, if your character was known to me onely as a Learned Man; for those who are far advanced in Learned Studies, and high speculations may think themselves excused from such a Condescention; but you I am confident would not contemne $^{261}$ the most Ignorant Lover of Truth; were I not secured by my sex of a favourable distinction from the obligeing civilitie of a man conversant in courts. I take the libertie therefore to request the favour of you that you will by some explication or definition of them help me to conceive what your Formes are; for I cannot but desire to understand a systeme recommended to me not onely by the eminence of its Author, but

content: ## 3.3.3 Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz to Damaris Masham, May 1704; in Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Bibliothek: Niedersächsische Landesbibliothek zu Hannover, LBr.612, fols.5-7.

label: text
content: Hanover, the beginning of May 1704

label: text
content: My Lady,

label: text
content: As I was receiving the honour of your request via a precious response from your hand, I was also given the good news that your present, for which I consider myself infinitely honoured, has fortunately made its way across the sea; and as such I hope to be able to enjoy it soon, as I have desired it more than once. I suspect that the book of the Intellectual System, with which you have had the kindness, Madam, to include a discourse by the same illustrious Author concerning very important Theological matters $^{266}$

His response to Masham's request (3.3.3) touches on a number of the points he makes in this reply. Although the 'Reply' was not published till 1716, it was written earlier, in 1702.

label: text
content: (for which you have increased my obligation), cannot be found in this country nor in any neighbouring country because of its language. It would be all the more important for me to re-read this system, since I have been thinking of conducting a review of my thoughts on similar subjects for quite a while. This would put me in a better position to satisfy your demands.I will nevertheless make an effort to comply without delay, which I pray you take as a sign of my gratitude, rather than the effect of an assurance that might merit censure.

label: text
content: Since I am completely in favour of the Principle of Uniformity, which I believe Nature observes in the depths of things, while varying in its ways, degrees, and perfections, my entire Hypothesis comes down to recognizing in imperceptible and unobservable substances something proportional to what can be observed in those things within our reach. Hence, assuming for the moment that there is in us a simple Being endowed with Action and Perception, I find that Nature would be scarcely unified if the particle of matter making up human bodies were the only one endowed with features that make it infinitely different to the rest (even physically) and completely heterogeneous with respect to all other known bodies. From this, I infer that there are such Beings active in Matter everywhere, and that they differ from one another only in their manner of perception. And since our own perceptions are sometimes accompanied by Reflection, and sometimes not, and since reflection gives rise to Abstractions and the Universal and Necessary Truths, whose vestiges we do not observe in beasts, and even less in other bodies surrounding us, there is reason to believe that the simple Being in us which we call 'Soul' differs from that of other known bodies by virtue of this feature.

label: text
content: Whether these principles of Action and Perception be called Forms, Entelechies, Souls or Minds $^{267}$ or whether one distinguishes these Terms according to the Notions that one would like to attribute to them, changes nothing. One may ask what will become of these simple Beings or souls that I see in beasts and other organic creatures; I would answer that they must be no less inextinguishable than our own and just as incapable of being produced or destroyed by the forces of Nature.

label: footnote
content: 267 Here and throughout this letter, Leibniz reiterates the metaphysical views expressed in his 'New System'. In that work, Leibniz refers to the 'substantial forms', the 'first entelechies', and the 'material souls' of Aristotelian scholastic philosophy—principles that purportedly explain the action and perception of animals (Leibniz's New System', pp. 12, 13). Rather than discard these discredited notions, Leibniz proposes to rehabilitate them and make them intelligible in his own philosophy.

label: text
content: But, to better preserve the analogy between the past or future, as well as other bodies, and what we presently experience in our own body, I maintain not only that these Souls or Entelechies all possess some manner of organic body proportionate to their perceptions, but that they will always have and have always had one for as long as they have existed; such that not only the soul, but also the animal itself (or whatever is analogous to the soul and the animal, to avoid disputing names) endures, and thus birth and death can be nothing more than developments and envelopments of which nature gives us but visible samples, as is her custom, so that we may surmise what she keeps hidden. And as a result, neither iron nor fire, nor all of the other violences of nature, whatever the damage they inflict on the animal body, could stop the soul from keeping a certain organic body, since the Organism, that is to say, the order and the artifice, is something essential to the matter produced and arranged by the sovereign wisdom, as the product must always keep a trace of its author. This also leads me to believe that there is no Mind entirely separate from Matter, save for the first sovereign Being, and that Spirits, however marvellous they could be, are always accompanied by bodies worthy of them. The same must be said about souls that one can nevertheless call separate in relation to this brute body. You can see, then, Madam, that all of this is only to suppose that it is everywhere and always the same as it is with us at this present time $^{268}$ (the supernatural aside), except for the varying degrees of perfection. And I leave you to judge if it is possible to come up with a simpler, at least, and more intelligible Hypothesis.

label: text
content: This same maxim, which says that one should never unnecessarily impute Creatures more than meets our own experience, also led me to my System of Pre-Established Harmony. For, in our experience, bodies interact with one another according to mechanical laws, and souls produce in themselves some kind of internal action. And we see no means of conceiving the Soul's Action on Matter, or of the Matter on the soul, nor anything that would correspond to it, as there is no mechanism whatsoever that could explain how material variations, that is to say, mechanical laws, can give rise to perception, or how perception can give rise to a change in velocity or direction in animal spirits and other bodies, however subtle or brute they may be. Thus,

For Leibniz's letter to Sophie Charlotte, see Lloyd Strickland (ed. and trans.), Leibniz and the Two Sophies: The Philosophical Correspondence (Toronto: Iter and Centre for Reformation and Renaissance Studies, 2011), pp. 310-17 (p. 311).

label: text
content: the inconceivability of any other Hypothesis, together with the idea of the right order of nature, which is always uniform in herself (leaving aside any other consideration), have led me to conclude that the soul and the body perfectly follow their laws, each according to its own, without the bodily laws being disturbed by the Actions of the soul, or presuming that the body finds windows through which its influence over the souls could enter. One must ask, therefore, where does this accord between the body and the soul come from? Proponents of occasional causes $^{269}$ hold that God reconciles from time to time the soul with the body, and the body with the soul. But that would be nothing short of miraculous and, therefore, incommensurable with a philosophy that must explain the ordinary course of nature, because it would entail that God must continually disturb the natural laws governing bodies. That's why I believe it infinitely worthier of God's Economy, and the uniformity and constant order of his work, to conclude that He first created souls and bodies such that each, following its own laws, matches the other. What one finds impossible is not so for a being whose wisdom and power are infinite. As such, I am merely attributing to Souls and bodies, always and everywhere, what one grasps in them whenever the experience is distinct—that is to say, the mechanical laws in bodies, and the internal Actions in the soul; and everything is simply the present state combined with the tendency to change, which takes place in the body by the moving forces, and in the soul following perceptions of good and evil.

label: text
content: The surprising thing that follows from all this is that the Works of God are infinitely more beautiful and harmonious than we believed. And one can say that the subterfuge used by the Epicureans against the argument drawn from the beauty of visible things (when they say that, in an infinity of chance productions, it is not amazing to find that some world, like ours, has passably succeeded) $^{270}$ is destroyed, inasmuch as the eternal correspondence amongst Beings that have no influence on each other can only come from

label: footnote
content: 269 Leibniz refers to the French philosopher-theologian Nicolas Malebranche (1638-1715). According to Malebranche's theory of occasionalism, the body has no causal influence over the soul (or vice versa); instead bodily states merely provide the 'occasions' for God to intervene and bring about modifications in the soul.

label: footnote
content: 270 The Epicureans were a group of ancient atomist philosophers, headed by the Greek thinker Epicurus (341-270 BCE). The later Roman Epicurean Lucretius writes that 'For so many primary particles have for an infinity of time past been propelled in manifold ways by impacts and by their own weight, and have habitually travelled, combined in all possible ways, and tried out everything that their union could create, that it is not surprising if they have also fallen into arrangements, and arrived at patterns of motion, like those repeatedly enacted by the present world'; see A. A. Long and D. N. Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers: Volume 1 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2014), 13F, pp.59-60.

label: text
content: a common cause of this harmony. Having contemplated the consequences of this Hypothesis, Mr Bayle (who is very thoughtful) recognized that the idea of the divine perfections has never been held in higher regard, and that the infinite wisdom of God, great as it is, is not too great to produce this preestablished harmony, whose possibility he seemed to doubt. $^{271}$ But I made him consider the fact that even men produce automata which act as if they were rational, $^{272}$ and that God (who is an Artist infinitely greater, or rather for whom all is art to the highest degree) laid out a path in matter to make it act as minds require it to. And so, after that, one must be no more surprised that matter acts so rationally than one would be at seeing the trajectory of certain firework rockets along the length of an invisible cord that make it seem like it is a man that leads them. $^{273}$ We will only grasp the designs of God through the perfections we discern in them. Just as bodies are in advance subject to souls in order to accommodate themselves over time to their voluntary actions, so the soul, in turn, is expressive of bodies by virtue of its primordial nature, having to represent them by its involuntary and confused perceptions. And so, each is the original or the copy of the other, relative to the perfections or imperfections it comprises.

label: text
content: But I almost forgot that I have the honour of writing to you, Madam, and this thought prompts me to ask your pardon for allowing myself to be so prolix. I should think few words suffice for your discernment and what could only be explained to you with legions of words would normally be something quite unintelligible; but having started, one is not the master of the ending, and I thought that it was better to be found lacking by excess. Moreover, I would be happy with my verbosity, if I had omitted nothing from what I wanted to say.

label: text
content: My happiness has been doubled, Madam, by the fact that you have won me the favour of a new token of kindness from an esteemed author of such renown as Mr Locke, who is so much more advanced in the honour of your acquaintance: I don't know if I ought to dare to beg you to transmit my highest esteem to him, and my wish to be worthy of his approbation or

label: footnote
content: 271 In his Remark L, Bayle praises Leibniz's system of pre-established harmony, noting that 'nothing can be imagined which gives so exalted an idea of the power and intelligence of the author of all things' (Leibniz's 'New System', p. 86). But then Bayle adds that he cannot see how pre-established harmony is at all possible.

label: footnote
content: 272 In his published and unpublished replies to Bayle, Leibniz refers to an automaton that is made to look and act like a servant, and also a machine capable of walking down the street and turning precisely at street corners (Leibniz's 'New System', pp. 98, 108-9).

label: footnote
content: 273 In his 'Reply' to Bayle, Leibniz similarly observes that the regulation of natural mechanisms is no stranger than 'a rocket (fusée) which runs (coule) along a rope' (Leibniz's New System', p. 110).

And as it is easier to continue on from what a clever man has started, it seems to me that I am in the position to raise a few difficulties and to fill certain gaps. One will be able to conclude whether I have reason to thus flatter myself by the outline of it that I have just given you in this letter, Madam. But I dare not flatter myself in thinking that I can satisfy a mind as discerning as yours, and it will be an achievement if there is something here that does not displease you. Your judgment thereon will illuminate mine, and will increase the obligation that I am under, being with all the respect and veneration that one is capable of,
