label: text
content: Sir,

label: text
content: Your great Civilitie Obliges me not the less for haveing presumed from your Goodness upon more than I had any Right to Pretend to when I requested you would give your Self the Pains of informing me farther Concerning your Hypothesis. To a Mind Possessed in any measure with a Due Admiration of the works of God Nothing is more Gratefull than by farther discoveries therein of his Divine Perfections, to be sensibly engaged to Adore that Being which Reason Pronounces ought to be the supreme object of our Affections.

label: text
content: An Hypothesis thought by your self and others conduceing to such an End as this, could not but excite my enquirie; and it did so the more because that in reading what you have Published, it seemed to my self also you had views there in which gave a Becomeing Idea of the Wisdome of God in his Works. The letter you have favoured me with confirms me in this Thought: but that I may be sure of having a certain and cleare knowledge of your Hypothesis permit me to tell you what I conceive it to be; in hopes you will rectifie my Mistakes if I am in any; which is what may easilie happen to one so little conversant as I am in such Speculations.

label: text
content: You take for granted that there is a Simple Being in us induced with Action and Perception. $^{276}$ The same, you say, differing onely in the manner of Perception, is in matter everie where. That that Simple Being in us, which is called Soul is distinguished from that of Beasts (and yet more from that of other Bodys about us) by the Power of Abstraction and frameing thereby Universal Ideas. All these Simple Beings you think have; Always will have; and ever since they existed have had Organick Bodys; proportioned to theire Perception. So that not onely after Death the Soul dos remain: but even the Animal also. Generation, and Death, being but a displaying or concealment of these Beings to, or from our view. The same Principle of Uniformitie in the works of Nature which has led you to beleeve this has, you say, led you also to your Systeme of the Harmonie Preestablished betweene Substances the which I thus understand.

label: text
content: Any Action of the Soul upon Matter, or of Matter upon the Soul is Inconceivable: these two have theire Laws distinct. Bodies follow the Laws of Mechanisme, and have a tendencie to change suivant les Forces Mouvantes. $^{277}$ Souls produce in themselves Internal Actions and have a tendencie to change according to the Perception that they have of Good or Ill. Now Soul and Body following each theire Proper Laws, and neither of them acting thereby upon or Affecting the other, such Effects are yet produced from a Harmonie Preestablished betwixt these Substances, as if there was a real communication betweene them. So that the Body acting constantly by its owne Laws of Mechanisme without receiving any variation or change therein from any Action of the Soul dos yet always correspond to the Passions and Perceptions which the soul hath. And the Soul in Like Manner, though not operated upon by the Motions of Matter, has yet at the same time that the Body Acts

label: footnote
content: 276 Masham's italicized remarks repeat Leibniz's sentiments from his previous letter (3.3.3).

label: footnote
content: $^{277}$ suivant les Forces Mouvantes] by the moving forces.

label: text
content: This is what I conceive you to say; in which (to tell you Thoughts so insignificant as mine) I see nothing, Peculiar, which seems not possible. I find a Uniformitie in it which pleases me: and the Advantages proposed from this Hypothesis are very Desirable. But it appears not yet to me that this is more than an Hypothesis; for as Gods ways are not limited by our conceptions; the unintelligibleness or inconceivableness by us of any way but one, does not methinks, much induce a Beleefe of that's being the way which God has chosen to make use of. Yet such an inference as this from our Ignorance, I remember P. Malbranche (or some other assertor of his Hypothesis) $^{278}$ would make in behalf of Occasional Causes: to which Hypothesis, amongst other exceptions, I think there is one, which I cannot without your help see, but that yours is alike Liable to and that is from the Organization of the Body: wherin all that Nice Curiositie that is discoverable seeming useless; becomes Superfluous, and Lost labour. $^{279}$ To this difficultie likewise let me add that I conceive not why Organisme should be or can be thought, as you say it is, Essential to Matter.

label: text
content: But these enquiries, or Others, that might it may be on further thoughts occur to me, are less Pertinent for me to make, than such a one as is more fundamental, although it dos not peculiarly respect your Hypothesis.

label: text
content: Forms, explained by you to signifie Simple Beings, you elsewhere call Atomes de Substance $^{280}$ and Forces Primitives,the nature whereof you, in another place say,you find to Consist in Force. Force (I presume) cannot be the essence of any Substance, but is the attribute of what you call a Form; Soul; or Atome de Substance, of the essence whereof I find no Positive Idea, $^{281}$ and your negation of theire having any Dimensions,makes theire Existence (I

label: footnote
content: 278 Masham refers to Pere (Father) Nicolas Malebranche and most likely John Norris, his English disciple. Masham wrote a critique of the moral implications of Malebranchean occasionalism in her anonymous Discourse Concerning the Love of God, a work specifically targeted against Norris.

label: footnote
content: 279 In her Discourse, Masham voices a similar criticism of Malebranchean occasionalism. She says that one consequence of the doctrine is that 'the Wisdom of God cannot herein be equally admired because it is not equally conspicuous. For if God immediately exhibits to me all my Idea's, and that I do not truly see with my Eyes, and hear with my Ears; then all that Wonderful Exactness and curious Workmanship, in framing the Organs of Sense, seems superfluous and vain; Which is no small reflection upon infinite Wisdom' (Masham, Discourse, pp. 31-2).

label: footnote
content: $^{280}$ Correction in manuscript: from 'Atomes des Substances' to 'Atomes de Substance'. Here Masham refers to a concept from Leibniz's 'New System' (Leibniz's 'New System', p.16). Leibniz's atoms of substance are real unities without parts, the basic constituents of things.

label: footnote
content: 281 Here Masham takes a somewhat Lockean approach to the concept of a 'real essence', the essence that makes something the thing that it is. In his Essay II.xxxi.6, Locke, too, maintains that we have no distinct idea of the real essence of substances.

label: text
content: confess) inconceivable to me; as not being able to conceive an existence of that which is No Where. $^{282}$ If the Localitie of these substances were accounted for by theire being as you [say] they are always in Organized Bodies, then they are somewhere: But if these Atomes de substance $^{283}$ are somewhere then they must have some extension, which you deny of them, who (I think) also place the Union of the Soul with its respective Body in Nothing else but that Correspondence or Conformitie whereby, in virtue of a Preestablished Harmonie, Souls and Bodys Acting apart, each by theire own Laws, the same effects are Produced as if theire was a real Communication betwixt them, Though whether or no I perfectly comprehend your meaning in this Part I am in Doubt.

label: text
content: What I have here said I think enough for me to venture to trouble you with at once: and it will perhaps be more than enough to show you that you have Judged by much too favourably of my Apprehension. For I remember my Father as well as other Assertors of unextended substance to have said That it is an imposition of Imagination upon theire Reason in Those who cannot be convinced of the reality of Substances unextended. $^{284}$ So great Authoritie as His was to me could not hinder me, if this be so, from being always under such an influence of Imagination; which is <what> I would not willingly be in any case. But wherever I have no Idea of a thing; or Demonstration of the Truth of any Proposition, the Truth of which is inconceivable by me, I cannot and conclude, that I ought not to assent to what is asserted of either: since should I once do this I know not where I should stop; what should be the Boundaries of Assent. Or why I might not Beleeve alike one thing as well as another.

label: text
content: Mr Locke presents you his humble service and desires me to tell you He takes himself to be mightilie obliged to you for your great Civilitie expressed to him; in which he finds you a master as well as in Philosophy and every thing else. His want of Health he says now, and the little remains he counts he has of Life, has put an end to his enquiries into Philosophical Speculations: though if he were still in the heat of that Pursuit he could not be

content: 282 Here Masham expresses a view that is close to that of her father's colleague Henry More. In the preface to his Immortality of the Soul (1659), More argues that whatever exists must have extension in some measure or other; otherwise it would be a pure negation or nonentity. He maintains that we can conceive of two types of extended substance: one that is active, penetrable, and indivisible (spiritual substance) and another that is passive, impenetrable, and divisible (material substance).

label: text
content: Hanover, 30 June 1704

label: text
content: My Lady,

label: text
content: I see that your kindness has made my letter seem acceptable, even though I was only too aware in writing it how insufficient it was in giving satisfaction to a Lady whose discernment is so fine. Having noticed it even more in your reply, where clarity and authority are joined with an extraordinary depth, I am even harder pressed to succeed in what I am going to write. But the honour of your request reassures me, and will at least excuse me.

label: text
content: You make the effort, Madam, to first summarize my Hypothesis, to allow me to judge if you have understood it well. This is a very useful method in these sorts of exchanges, and I admire the accuracy and precision of your

label: text
content: expression in such an abstract subject. So much so, that I will profit from it myself on another occasion when I need to explain myself to someone.

label: text
content: Having done so, you move on to reflecting upon these matters. These reflections are certainly a merit to you, and deserve the effort to take them into account and adapt my notions. You also praise my Hypothesis for being plausible, for observing the uniformity of nature, and even for conforming with our desires.

label: text
content: But you added, Madam, that it does not yet seem anything more than a Hypothesis. $^{285}$ And even though it might seem more conceivable than other Hypotheses, it is not by necessity true, since the ways of God are not limited by our conceptions. And even if all other ways, except one, seem unintelligible and inconceivable, this sole way is not thereby demonstratively proven to be the correct one.

label: text
content: To add my comments to yours, as you request, I would say (1) that it is seemingly a considerable thing that a hypothesis appears possible when all others do not, and (2) that it is extremely probable that such a hypothesis is the true one. So it has always been recognized in Astronomy and Physics that the most intelligible hypotheses are, in the end, found to be the true ones: such as that of the movement of the earth to save the appearances of the Stars, and that of the weight of the air, to give reason for air pumps and other attractions that we once attributed to the fear of the void.

label: text
content: Moreover (3), since our Understanding comes from God, and must be considered as a beam from this sun, we are justified in thinking that what is most consistent with our understanding (when one proceeds in an orderly fashion, and as the nature itself of the understanding demands) is also consistent with the divine wisdom; and that judging according to this method, we follow the orders that God has given us. Therefore, we have always found (4) that our judgments, when they have been made according to his natural light, so to speak, have never been contradicted by events; and the oppositions that the sceptics have mounted against this view have always been taken by reasonable people as mind games.

label: text
content: But, more to the point, (5) it is useful to consider that the Ways of God are of two types: one natural, and the other extraordinary or miraculous. The natural ones are always those that a created mind could conceive, if it had the requisite opening and occasion to do so; but the miraculous ways are beyond all created minds. Thus, the operation of the magnet is natural, being

label: footnote
content: 285 Leibniz repeats Masham's sentiments from her previous letter (3.3.4).

label: text
content: mechanical or explicable, even though we may still lack the means to explain it perfectly in detail. But if someone claimed that the magnet does not operate mechanically, and that it does everything by a pure attraction from afar, without means or medium, and without visible or invisible instruments, it would be a wondrous thing, inexplicable to all created minds, however informed or perceptive. In a word, it would be something miraculous. Yet, the reason and order of divine wisdom itself does not want us to resort to miracles without necessity. The same could be said here about the system of the soul's union with the body, since saying that a body operates at a distance without means and instruments is no better, as far as explanations go, than saying that completely different substances like the soul and the body affect each other immediately, given that the gap between natures is even greater than that between any two places. Such that the communication between these two heterogeneous substances, no less than the immediate communication of two distant bodies, could only be achieved by miracle. To want to attribute this communication to some mysterious influence of one over the other, is to hide the miracle under words that signify nothing. The same applies to the theory of occasional causes, with the sole difference that a perpetual miracle is introduced by the authors of this theory, not covertly, as in the theory of influence, but openly, whether they admit it or not. For although this action of God of occasionally moving the soul towards the body, and the body towards the soul, would be continuous and common, it would be no less miraculous. $^{286}$ It would always be something inexplicable to all created spirits, no matter how informed they are or what opportunity God may have given them, insofar as this effect would only depend on the immediate operation of God, without offering any other means or explanation. The authors of this theory admit that God would thus continually interfere with the laws of the body in order to make it adapt to the soul, and vice versa, rather than accepting that what is explicable conforms with the natural laws of things, and must be explained only by them.

label: text
content: Thus (6) it seems that my Hypothesis is something more than a Hypothesis, quite simply being not only possible, but also more compatible with the wisdom of God, and the order of things. And I believe that one can say with certainty that God always operates in the way that is most suitable

label: footnote

label: text
content: to his perfections, of which wisdom is one of the greatest. Yet, it is plain that nothing is more beautiful or better governed than this thoughtful accord that God established in natural things, and nothing is a better mark of his creation, for it is worthy of him to regulate everything in advance so that nothing need be done in the future that goes against his rules which conform with the nature of things. Neither would it be possible that, by themselves, they accorded so perfectly by pre-established harmony, if they did not come from a common cause and if this cause was not infinitely powerful and provident so as to be able to extend itself to all things so rightfully.

label: text
content: And what is more, (7) supposing that ordinary things must be done naturally, and not by miracle, it seems that, as a result, one can say that my Hypothesis is proven, as the two other hypotheses must necessarily appeal to miracles, as I just showed in (5). And, in all, there are no hypotheses other than these three. For either the laws of bodies and souls are interfered with, or else they are maintained. If these laws are interfered with (which could only happen from the outside), then either one of these two things must disturb the other, which is the hypothesis of influence, quite common in the schools; or it is a third party which disturbs them, that is to say God, as in the hypothesis of occasional causes. Finally, if the laws of souls and bodies are maintained without being disturbed, then this is the hypothesis of pre-established harmony, which is consequently the only natural one.

label: text
content: (8) This preference that must be given to the natural above the miraculous in ordinary interactions of nature, about which I believe all philosophers (apart from some half-fanatics like Fludd $^{287}$ in his Mosaic philosophy) have been in agreement so far; this preference, I say, is also reason for holding that it is not matter which thinks, but a simple being that is apart or independent, and joined to the matter. It is true that the illustrious Mr Locke held in his excellent Essay, and in writing against the late Bishop of Worcester, that God could give matter the power to think, because he can do things that go beyond that which we can conceive; $^{288}$ but it would therefore be by perpetual

label: footnote
content: 287 Robert Fludd (1574-1637), English physician and occult philosopher. In his Mosaicall Philosophy (1659), he puts forward the view that God operates in every part of nature, giving life and motion to all created things.

label: footnote
content: 288 Leibniz refers to Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding and Locke's 1697 and 1698 published replies to Edward Stillingfleet, Bishop of Worcester. In Essay IV.iii.6, Locke puts forward the view that, on the basis of our ideas of 'matter' and 'thought' alone, we cannot know that an all-powerful God has not bestowed the power of thinking on some systems of matter. In response, Stillingfleet claims that if it is conceivable that God can super-add thought to matter, then a crucial argument for the immortality of the soul is undermined—an argument that rests upon the soul's immateriality. In his 1698 Reply, Locke answers this objection by pointing out that it is entirely conceivable that God might bestow immortality on a material as well as an immaterial substance.

label: text
content: miracle that matter should be able to think, as there is nothing in matter itself, that is to say, in extension and impenetrability, from which thought could be deduced or upon which it could be founded. One can therefore say that the natural immortality of the soul is proven, and that one would not be able to maintain the idea of its extinction except by miracle, either by attributing to matter an ability to think, miraculously attained and maintained, in which case the soul could die with the cessation of the miracle, or by claiming that the thinking substance, distinct from the body, could be annihilated, which would still be miraculous, but by a new miracle. Yet, I say that God, in this case of the thinking matter, must not only give matter the capacity to think, but also maintain it there continually by the same miracle, since thinking has no root in matter, unless God gives matter a new nature. But if one said that God gave matter this new nature or the radical power to think, which then maintained itself by itself, it would in fact be a thinking soul that He gave to it, or else something which differs only in name; and as this radical power would not properly be a modification of matter (since modifications are explicable by the natures that they modify, whereas this power is not), it would be independent of matter.

label: text
content: Next, Madam, I come to some major problems that have occurred to you. You note that (9) the organs seem to serve no purpose if the soul is sufficient. I respond by saying that if the soul of Cesar (for example) had to be alone in nature, the Author of things could have done without giving him organs. But this same author wanted to make an infinity of other beings, which are enveloped in one another's organs. Our body is a type of world full of an infinity of creatures which also deserve to exist, and if our body were not organized, our microcosm or small world couldn't have all the perfection that it should have, and the big World would not be as rich as it is.

label: text
content: (10) Also on this basis, I said provisionally that the organism is essential to matter, but only to matter arranged by a sovereign wisdom. And it is for this reason too that I define the Organism, or the natural machine, as a machine whose parts are also machines, and consequently as one whose subtle structure goes on into infinity, wherein nothing is small enough to be neglected, whereas the parts of our artificial machines are not themselves machines. Herein lies the essential difference between nature and art, which our moderns have not sufficiently considered.

label: text
content: For further details on the Locke-Stillingfleet debate, see Elizabeth Burnet's letters to Locke in chapter 4 of this volume.

label: text
content: (11) It also seems to you, Madam, that the Force could not be the essence of any substance. This is undoubtedly because you are talking about changeable forces, in the common sense, whereas by primitive Force I understand the Principle of Action, of which the changeable forces are only modifications.

label: text
content: (12) The positive idea of this simple substance or primitive force, because it must always have in it a regulated progression of perceptions, was found by following the Analogy that it must have with our soul.

label: text
content: (13) The question whether it [the Soul] is somewhere or nowhere, is merely verbal, since its nature does not consist in extension. Instead, it relates to the extension it represents, and therefore one must place the soul in the body, which furnishes the vantage from which the soul represents the universe in the present. Wanting something more and placing souls in dimensions, is tantamount to imagining souls as being like bodies.

label: text
content: (14) As for complete substances without extension, I agree with you, Madam, that there are none amongst the creatures. Souls or forms without bodies would be something incomplete, especially since, in my opinion, the soul is never without the animal, or something analogous. And God Himself is only known to us through an idea which comprises a relation to extension, that is to say, to a continuous and lawful variety of contemporary things that He has produced; therefore, it is only by its effects that we come to know His existence. But sovereign reason shows us later that there is something in Him beyond extension, which is its very source, as well as the source of every transformation that takes place in it; even though this is not something imaginable, we should not be surprised about it, for even mathematics gives us an infinity of things that we could not imagine—witness the incommensurables $^{289}$ whose truth is nevertheless demonstrated. This is why one must not balk at truths under the pretext that they are beyond the reach of the imagination. The limits of approval are not drawn by Imagination, and Mr Locke has clearly demonstrated that our ideas of reflection involve something beyond the impressions of our senses. $^{290}$

label: text
content: I am saddened, Madam, to hear of the poor health of this excellent person; those suffering the same would not be too long to live. If he is still at your side, this charming visit will be the best form of medicine that he can take; and the obligation that studious people will have towards you (me in particular, who

label: text
content: ## Sir

label: text
content: Whatever allowances are to be made for the Language of Civilitie to Ladys, differing but little from what would look like Flatterie to one of your own Sex; Yet I find a Pleasure in being Praised by You, which I Justifie to my self from a Beleefe that when you Honour me with such Expressions of your good opinion, you make me the Best return in Your Power for that Well Grounded Esteeme I have for you, by a Desire which that has created in you of finding me Worthy of Yours. Nor shall I ever reckon it a small matter if I have Desert enough to engage Those of a distinguished Merit to wish that I had more. Thus, if I do flatter my self, I am by a Vanitie but very little Moderated, or rather Refined beyond that of Others, Pleased with the favorable things you say of me, without that Cruel allay attending this Satisfaction which a Consciousness of not resembling the Picture you have made for me must otherwise give me.

label: text
content: Whether I have rightly represented your Systeme you Best can tell: and what you say on that Subject I am Proud of; Whilst the Inferences you would draw from thence to my advantage can give me onely a Due acknowledgement for your wishing me so much fitter for your Correspondence than I am. But however justly I may have expressed your sense so far as I indeavoured to represent it, your Answers to some of my Enquiries makes me question whether I fully apprehended All that is included in your Hypothesis. For I do

label: text
content: not yet sufficiently see upon what you ground Organism's being Essential to Matter: or indeed very well understand your meaning in these words that Organisme is not absolutely Essential to Matter but to matter arrangée par une sagesse souveraine. $^{291}$ What you would Build upon this, Forms a very Transcendent Conception of the Divine Artifice; and such as I think could onely occur to the thoughts of one possessed with the highest admiration of the wisdome of his Maker: but if you infer the Truth of this Notion onely from its being the most agreeable one that you can Frame to that Attribute of God, this, singly, seems to me not to be concludeing; Since we can in my opinion only infer from thence that whatsoever God dos must be according to infinite Wisdom; but are not able with our short and narrow views to determine what the operations of an Infinitely Wise Being must be.

label: text
content: The Principle of Action called by you Force Primitive is you say a Substance; of the which, I still perceive not the positive Idea, Perception being but the Action of this Substance: what you add concerning its Perceptions, in these words, suivant l'Analogie qu'elle doit avoir avec notre ame, $^{292}$ makes me again believe that I do not fully understand your scheme: since I thought before that the Soul and this Force Primitive, or Principle of Action, had been the same thing. You say renfermer les Ames dans les Dimensions c'est Vouloir imaginer les ames Comme des Corps. $^{293}$ In regard of Extension this is true; and Extension is, to me, inseparable from the notion of All Substance. I am yet sensible that we ought not to reject Truths because they are not Imaginable by us (where there is ground to admit them). But Truth being but the attributeing certain affections conceived to belong to the subject in question, I can by no means attribute any thing to a subject whereof I have no conception at all; as I am conscious to my self I have not of Unextended Substance. What you instance in therefore of Lines Incommensurable seems not to me to answer the case; for I herein do conceive the Proposition, and have Cleare Ideas of Lines Incommensurable, though I do not see the reason of theire Incommensurabilitie: but of an unextended substance I have not any conception, from whence I can affirm, or Deny, any thing concerning it.

label: text
content: Why you think that theire is no created substance complete without Extension: or that the soul (which you suppose a distinct Substance) would without the Body be a Substance Incompleat without Extension, I understand not: but my owne Beleefe that there is no substance whatever unextended is (as I have alreadie said), grounded upon this that I have no conception of such a thing. I cannot yet but conceive two very different Substances to be in the universe, though Extension alike agrees to them Both. For I clearly conceive an Extension without Solidity, and a Solid Extension: to some system of which last if it should be affirmed that God did annex Thought, I see no absurdity in this from there being nothing in Extension and Impenetrabilitie (or Soliditie), from whence thought can naturally, or by a train of causes be derived; the which I Beleeve to be Demonstrable it cannot be. But that was never supposed by me; and my question in the case would be this; Whether God could not as conceivably by us as create an unextended Substance, and then unite it to an Extended Substance (wherin, by the way, there is methinks on your side two difficulties for one) whether God, I say, could not as conceivably by us as his Doing this would be, Add (if he so pleased) the Power of Thinking to that Substance which was Soliditie? Soliditie and Thought being both of them but attributes of some unknown substance and I see not why it may not be one and the same which is the common support of Both These; there appearing to me no Contradiction in a co-existence of Thought and Soliditie in the same substance. Neither can I apprehend it to be more Inexplicable that God should give Thought to a Substance which I know not, but whereof I know some of its attributes, than to another, supposed, Substance of whose very Being I have no conception at all, and that any substance whatsoever should have Thought belonging to it, or resulting from it, otherwise than as God has Willed it shall have so, I cannot Apprehend.

label: text
content: That God dos in frameing and Ordering of all his Works always make use of the most simple meanes I doubt not, this appearing to me the most suitable to his Wisdome, but whether or no, these simple meanes or methods are always such as surpass not a created intelligence, I do not know: but am very apt to Beleeve That Gods Ways are Past our finding out, in this sense.

label: text
content: I have no sooner scribled to you these Thoughts of Mine, than I feare wearying you by my Dulness. I shall therefore Wave taking notice of any thing more that has occured to me in considering the several Parts of your letter; or making any such farther inquiries as perhaps were these resolved, I might be able in some measure to cleare to my self. I will however now mention to you one difficultie (as I conceive) in your Hypothesis, which I think not

label: text
content: that I could ever extricate it from without your assistance and it is [t]o me a very material one. That is, how to reconcile Your Systeme to Liberty or Free Agencie: $^{294}$ for though in regard of any Compulsion from other causes, we are according thereto Free, yet I see not how we can be so in respect of the first Mover. This I omitted takeing notice of in my last not onely because I thought it too remote an inquiry for one who wanted to be inlightened concerning the very foundation you Built upon: but also because I must acknowledge that I cannot make out Libertie either with or without any Hypothesis whatsoever. Though as being persuaded that I feel myself a Free Agent and that Freedome to Act is necessarie to our being Accountable for our Actions, I not onelie conclude we are induced therewith, but am very tenacious hereof: whence I should be sorry to find from any new Hypothesis new difficulties in maintaining of this. I think not much that I need seek to Justifie to you the part which I own my Inclination has in this opinion; since what you have said in print persuades me that you have the same Beleef with the same Bias. I might else (perhaps) alledge (in my excuse at least) that as I am a True English Woman, I cannot but naturally have a passion for Libertie in All senses wherein I consider it: and I would not have so much as the Philosophy of Hanover Unfavourable to any Kind of it.

label: text
content: What you write on the subject of Mr Locke's health, he is much obliged by: and I am no less so when you recommend to me the care of one of the Best Freinds I have in the World as a matter in which you interest your self. If I could contribute to the prolonging so valuable a Life as his, I should think this one of the best uses I could ever make of my own. He is not onely still with me, but in all Probabilitie will never have health enough to permit him the thoughts of Leaving any more a Place which he has made Agreable to Others by having for so many years chosen to spend therein a great Part of his time. Rational Conversation with Mutual Good Will, has the greatest Charmes that I know in Life, and I have hitherto been very Happy in respect of that Enjoyment. $^{295}$ To my Felicitie in which kind I think it a considerable

label: text

label: text
content: Though I owe you greatly for your kindness, it is not out of gratitude that I noted the satisfaction that your representation of my system gave me, but rather because I sincerely felt it. I would be a flatterer, however, if I pretended that you had penetrated all the layers, which is something I have not yet done myself. Your difficulties, however, signal the intelligence you have regarding this matter, as they are significant and worthy of being resolved.

label: text
content: When I said that the organism is essential to matter arranged by a divine wisdom, you doubted, Madam, whether we could determine by reflection how this infinite wisdom operates; I answer that, although we cannot determine its operations in detail, we can nevertheless accomplish this kind of reflection in a general sense by excluding everything that does not conform to it. Thus, supposing that there is nothing careless or barren in the works of God, the Atoms, for example, would not be able to exist, as there is no variety or qualitative detail in their parts, which is a flaw incompatible with divine Architecture. One must protect oneself from a clever Pyrrhonism, $^{296}$ hidden under a false modesty, which would stretch too far the truth that we do not know enough about the ways of God. It is like those who give themselves the liberty of attributing tyrannical Actions to God, under the pretext that the rules of divine justice can sometimes go beyond us.

label: footnote
content: 296 Pyrrhonism] a form of scepticism, first promulgated by Pyrrho of Elis (360 BCE-270 BCE) in ancient Greece.

label: text
content: It is perhaps a terminological question, whether all Entelechies ought to be called Souls. It all depends on the definitions that we would want to give to these terms.

label: text
content: One must conceive some substance without extension, for God, again cannot be extended. But I claim that all created substances are accompanied by extension and I do not know any that are entirely separated from matter, as I mentioned to you earlier. This is the way to remove a thousand difficulties, though I do not wish thereby to dispute what is possible for God.

label: text
content: I am willing to admit, Madam, that you have no image of an unextended substance; but that does not prevent you from having an idea of it. Since Mr. Locke is of the same opinion, judging by his Essay, $^{297}$ and lives in your home, it would be wrong of me to undertake what he can do better and from nearby.

label: text
content: <sup>298</sup>As you have some notion of substance, and of something unextended too (for instance, of a point), you have, despite your great humility, a notion of unextended substance. It is true that it is imperfect in us until we demonstrate, through an analysis of these notions, whether they are compatible or not. But if we didn't have any conceptions until we had a sufficient Analysis of them, many Geometricians would not even have the conception of the straight line. For it is important to know that the image we have of it is not the distinct idea of a straight line, and does not suffice for demonstrating its properties. Because we don't consider this sufficiently, we create difficulties for ourselves where there are none, and believe that we cannot conceive what we do conceive, and vice versa. Supposing, Madam, that you were unable to comprehend the reasoning behind the incommensurability of lines, you would have no clearer an idea of it than that which you have of an unextended substance, for in that case you could not determine, based on its idea alone, whether the substance or the line is possible, to wit, distinctly conceivable, or not. It is the logic of possibility that decides the clarity of intellectual ideas.>

label: text

An Atom would be an incomplete substantial thing as would a soul without a body, or a body without a soul; the same holds for an extension without solidity. It would be like a number without things that

label: text
content: <Strictly speaking, solid extension without a soul is only the result of several substances, and by no means a true substance.>

label: text
content: [<]Thus, in my system, matter which thinks without a soul can only be an impossible fiction or, at most, a miracle; it is true to say that there is a substance which has thought and extension at the same time, if by 'substance' one means the compound of soul and body, for example, man; but if one means the simple substance, it is clear that it could not have extension in itself, since all extension is composite.>

label: text
content: With regards to liberty, I don't see that there is any more difficulty about it in my system than in the others, and as Mr Locke has written such a wonderful chapter on the subject, it would be unbecoming of me to try to add to the Ephod $^{299}$ or domestic oracle that you have, Madam. Thus, I would only say this to you with respect to my system: when it comes to freedom, which demands that we act with spontaneity and with choice, my system increases our spontaneity and does not diminish our choice.

label: text
content: Madam, I greatly partake in the satisfaction that you have—and are giving us too—in seeing to the preservation of our illustrious Mr Locke. I hope that your care in this and all other things be fruitful, and I am with respect,

label: text
content: It being a long while since the date of your First Letter to me, though not very long since I received it; the High Value that I have for the Honour of your Correspondence makes me fear incuring the suspicion of a neglect I can never be Guiltie of in your regard; and induces me now to write, though the loss I have but lately had; and since that the solicitous Care which attends the first sending an onely Child into the World under his own Conduct, dos at present much indispose me.

label: text
content: Yours of the 16th of September came not to my Hands till our 31 of October: the day wherin was Performed the last office to one that had been my Freind above half my life time. Mr Locke I meane. $^{301}$ A Freind who though very accidentally <an Acquaintance> and Perfectly unknown to my Familie, has supplyd to me the Place of a Father and Brother: and to whose Direction, next to the Favour of God, I cheifly ascribe it if my Son (as I have reason to Hope) be blessed with a Sound Mind in a Sound Body. But this has been but the Best Effect of Mr Locks Freindship, not the onely one: for he has in his last will left to my Son (or in case of his Death to myself) a legacie in

label: footnote

He does not engage in any further philosophical inquiry into the subject, because this would go too far beyond 'the notions on which the philosophy now in the world is built' (Essay IV.x.18).

label: text

That This is less Inconceivable than the Creation of an Immaterial Substance was what I imagined before I knew Mr Locke, which has made me, perhaps, more inadvertant than I should else have been to what he intimates in the Chapter you cite.

label: text
content: Not long since, the Library Keeper of the Universitie of Oxford desired of Mr Locke, for the Bodleian Library, the Books of which he was the Author. Mr Locke in return to this request, presented to the said Library All the Books Published under his Name. But in a Codicil to his Will $^{303}$ he takes Notice that he had not been herein understood fully to have answered the request made him; it being supposed he was the Author of other Treatises to which his Name was not Prefixed. In Complyance therefore (he says) with what was desired in the utmost extent of it, and in acknowledgment of the Honour done him in thinking his Writeings worthy to be placed amongst the works of the Learned, in that August Repositorie; he dos further give to the Publick Library of the Universitie of Oxford these following Books—which are; Three letters Concerning Tolleration. Two Treatises of Government. The Reasonableness of Christianitie as delivered in the scriptures. A Vindication of the Reasonableness and so on <from Mr Edwards Reflections>. label: text
content: Hanover, 10 July 1705.

label: text
content: My Lady,

label: text
content: The death of the Queen of Prussia has caused a long interruption in my correspondence and my meditations. This great Princess showed me boundless kindness: she took pleasure in being informed about my speculations, even studying them in depth, and I shared with her the reports coming from you and that I had the honour of replying to you. We have perhaps never seen a Queen so accomplished and philosophical as she was. You can imagine the pleasure I felt, Madam, at being often in the company of such a Princess, and being encouraged by the passion she had for knowledge and truth. When she left for Hanover, I was supposed to follow her soon after, for she did me the honour of requesting my presence most often; but what a surprise it was to me, and indeed to all of Berlin, when we learned of her death! For me in particular, who suffered the biggest personal loss amongst the general public, it was like being struck by lightning. I thought I would become ill with grief, sensibility not being dependent on reason. I was profoundly upset by her death, but have finally recovered and returned to myself and my

label: footnote

label: text
content: I have not yet been able to give my condolences over the death of Mr Locke. It is a great loss for the public, and I see that you have had much reason to regret it personally. I am pleased to see that the public does justice to the merit of this great man, for though not everyone shares his speculative system, everyone ought to comply with his practical philosophy. What you have sent me regarding his death and his works has been forwarded to the collectors of the Leipzig Journal des savans, to put to good use. I thank you for it sincerely, and was very pleased to learn which works he has acknowledged as his own.

label: text
content: I once read The Reasonableness of Christianity by this illustrious Author, and strongly congratulate those who succeed in demonstrating the conformity of faith with reason. For my part, I believe one ought to take it as a maxim that unreasonableness is a sign of hypocrisy in Theology as well as in Philosophy.

label: text
content: I am vexed that he has taken with him the notion that he himself says is very different from the one we entertain, which made him believe that the creation of an immaterial substance is less conceivable. On my view, however, it is quite the contrary: strictly speaking, bodies cannot even be substances, since they are always aggregates or products of simple substances, or veritable monads, which cannot be extended and, consequently, cannot be bodies. Bodies, therefore, presuppose immaterial substances.

label: text
content: Your kindness, Madam, and that of Mr Locke, had led me to begin organizing some of the difficulties that I encountered while reading his Excellent Essay, $^{306}$ but his death has put me off, as I am no longer in a position to benefit from his clarifications. I see, however, that there are others who put forward their objections, such as Mr Sherlock $^{307}$ among others.

label: text
content: I am quite sympathetic to those who believe that the source of necessary truths is innate <in> our minds, [and that] experiences or observations of the senses can never prove that a truth is absolutely necessary or must always obtain. The intellectual system of the late Mr Cudworth comes back to me vividly. Like him, I am against the idea of fate and likewise hold that justice is natural, never arbitrary, and that God made things in such a way that they could be otherwise but not better; that the very constitution of bodies obliges

label: text
content: us to acknowledge immaterial substances; that the Hylozoist $^{308}$ hypothesis, which claims to draw life and sensation from matter, is untenable, and that it is not possible for sensation to arise from nothing; that souls are always united to some organic body, or rather, on my view, never entirely leave their organs; that, finally, incorporeal substance has an energy or internal active force. Regarding plastic nature, I believe in general, and agree with Mr Cudworth, that animals were not formed mechanically by something non-organic, $^{309}$ <as Democritus and Mr Descartes $^{310}$ believed>. But I also believe that this plastic force is itself mechanical, and consists in a preformation inhering in already existing organs, which were alone capable of forming other organs. So, I merely explain what Mr Cudworth left without explanation. Regarding Atoms, I allow them, but only in the sense of infinitesimal corpuscles; but if one holds them to be corpuscles which are infinitesimally solid, I do not allow them, since matter is plastic or organic everywhere, even in the tiniest portions that one can conceive of, and would not naturally contain the principle of an inseparable union of the parts within it; just as it could not bear the void which opposes the rule that things are made in the best way possible. But it is time to finish, noting with how much respect I am,

label: footnote
content: 308 Hylozoism is the theory that matter is endowed with life as part of its essence.

label: footnote
content: 309 Cudworth attributes a conscious life to animals and denies that all animal life and motion can be explained in mechanistic terms alone. His theory of plastic nature asserts that there is an inward immaterial principle pervading the natural world, capable of ordering and regulating material things for the sake of ends, but without self-perception and consciousness itself.

label: footnote
content: $^{310}$ The ancient Greek atomist Democritus (c.460-c.370 BCE) maintains that all the life and activity of animals can be explained in terms of the mechanical interactions of atoms. René Descartes (1596-1650) similarly maintains that all the behaviour of animals is explicable in terms of the mechanical principles of matter in motion.

content: Your Excuseing to me therefore your Silence is very obligeing as a mark of your putting a value on my Correspondence that it has no claim to: But the reason you give of your not haveing writ to me sooner has renewed in me a Sorrow which I could not but pertake in with all the World to whom were known (though but by Fame onely) the Great Endowments and Accomplishments of that Admirable Princess whose Death has so much Afflicted you. $^{311}$ One cannot have a deeper sense than I have of Your Particular Loss in this Universal One: and if ever Greif was Just yours must be allowed to be so.

label: text
content: The Experience of the Wisest dos I find on some occasions attest to this truth, that La sensibilité ne depend pas du Raisonnement. $^{312}$ There is however much difference betwixt them and others; in that if theire Reason does not always Triumph, it yet at least hinders Passion from doing so: and it is a Happy distinction not to be Led Captive by those Tyrants—under which the Generalitie of Mankind suffer a Worse Slaverie than the most Arbitrarie Masters can inflict.

label: text
content: I was Highly Honoured in having any Thoughts of mine communicated to the Queene of Prussia: but what you thought worth the answering I cannot wonder that she vouchsafed $^{313}$ a Hearing to.

label: text
content: I have flattered myself since my Last to you that (Possibly) within another yeare I might have the oopuntie to converse with you better than by Letters, in seeing you at Hanover: for if some whose Judgments I rely upon, had thought it fit for a Young Gentleman destined to the study of the Law $^{314}$ to spend a little Time first in Travelling, I should with his Fathers leave, Gladly have accompanied my Son in such a Voyage: both as proposing great Pleasure therein; and also as having been persuaded that Travelling would contribute to my Health, which has been much disordered this Last Yeare.

label: text
content: You have added to the many Reasons I have to Regret the Death of Mr Locke in leting me know that it will hinder the Publick from Profiting by your Remarks upon his Essay. The Debates of Those who equally search Truth cannot but be advantageous to the discoverie of it, or to the seting it in a Clearer Light: and which ever it be, both Parties in such cases will think themselves alike Gainers.

content: I am sorry with you that the Strength or Weakness of any Notion which you believe important to be known, should not be so. It were to be Wished that All who in respect of any Usefull Truth, have views beyond others would not neglect to communicate them, that so they may be out of danger of being Useless to the World. This should methinks induce you to oblige (as Mr Le Clerc $^{315}$ tells you you would do) all the Lovers of Philosophy, in explaining at Large your Systeme; whereby it being set in a Just Light, the advantages of it may neither be Lost; nor Prejudiced, by the unskilful representation that (it may be) some other Person who shall Less perfectly Comprehend it may some time, or other, venture to give of it. This I cannot but wish; and This I find some hope you will be Excited to by Mr Bayle's Reflection upon Your Sentiments amongst Those of others.

label: text
content: If you have read what has been writ betwixt him and Mr Le Clerc on the Subject of the Hypothesis of the Plastick Nature as asserted by my Father, $^{316}$ I should be very glad to know whether what Mr Bayle has offered dos amount to any thing more than a beging of the Question. $^{317}$ That God cannot make an unknowing Agent so as to Act to Wise Ends; yet without such his Perpetual Direction thereof as the Cartesian Hypothesis gives to Material Causes: for if it be conceivable for God to do so, but not conceivable for senseless Matter of it self to Act for Ends; my Fathers Hypothesis is methinks sufficiently secured from the Retorsion of Atheists, $^{318}$ without being in the same case with any one which makes God the immediate Efficient Cause of all the Effects of

label: footnote
content: 315 In volume 5 of his Bibliothèque choisie, Le Clerc encouraged Leibniz to enlarge on his system of pre-established harmony by way of comparison with Ralph Cudworth's doctrine of plastic nature. Leibniz eventually responded with his 'Considerations on Vital Principles and Plastic Natures, by the author of the pre-established harmony', published as a letter in Histoire des ouvrages des savants in May 1705. For this piece, see Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Philosophical Papers and Letters, translated and edited Leroy E. Loemker, 2nd edn (Dordrecht: Kluwer, 1989), pp. 586-91.

label: footnote
content: 316 From 1703 to 1706, Le Clerc published excerpts from Cudworth's True Intellectual System in his new French-language journal, Bibliothèque choisie. In response, Pierre Bayle published critiques of Cudworth's philosophy of nature: in Bayle's own Continuation des pensées diverses sur la comète (1705) and in Henri Basnage de Beauval's Histoire des ouvrages des savants. For Bayle's comments, see Oeuvres diverses de Mr. Pierre Bayle, 4 vols (La Haye: Par La Compagnie des Libraires, 1737), vol. iv, pp. 182-5. For Masham's letter to Le Clerc on this subject, see 3.2.3 in this present volume.

label: footnote
content: 317 In the final paragraph of his critique, Bayle comments on the fact that Le Clerc received a letter from Masham, in which she complained about Bayle's treatment of her father. In his defence, Bayle urges his readers to judge his comments by their own lights, and he likewise invites Masham to judge whether or not she has been misinformed about his critique (Bayle, Oeuvres, vol. iv, p. 185; see also Bayle's letters to Pierre Coste and Pierre Desmaizeaux, Oeuvres, vol. iv, pp. 857-9). This letter to Leibniz (3.3.11) might be regarded as Masham's response to Bayle's invitation.

label: footnote
content: 318 In his commentary on Cudworth, Bayle refers to 'la rétorsion des Athées' (Oeuvres, vol. iv, p. 183). Bayle suggests that the charge of atheism might be turned back against Cudworth's own system of nature.

content: Nature. $^{319}$ Since my Father dos not therein $^{320}$ assert (as Mr Bayle says he dos) That God has been able to give to Creatures a Facultie of Produceing Excellent Works (that is, such as is the Organization of Plants and Animals) seperate from all Knowledge $^{321}$ and so on: but Onely a Facultie of Executeing instrumentally his Ideas or Designs, in the Production of such Excellent Works: so that (according to him) there is (differently from what Mr Bayle asserts of his Hypothesis) an inseparable union betwixt the Power of produceing Excellent Works, and the Idea of theire Essence, and manner of produceing them. $^{322}$ [A]nd it [seems to] me that there can be no Pretence for the Retorsion of Atheists unless it were asserted, That God had been able to give to Creatures a Facultie of Produceing excellent Works, the Ideas whereof never were in any Understanding: But my Father is so far from asserting any such thing as this, that he holds the Operations of the Plastick Nature to be essentially and necessarilie Dependent on the Ideas in the Divine Intellect. $^{323}$ So that (I conceive) if Matter could be supposed to have of it self that same Power which Plastick Natures are said to have by the Gift of God, $^{324}$ it would not help the Atheists Cause at all: Because the Power given to Plastick Natures being onely a Power to Execute the Ideas of a Perfect Mind; if there were no Mind in the Universe; this Power in the Matter must Lye for ever Dormant, and unproductive, of any such Excellent Work as is spoken of.

label: text
content: Thus I see not in my Fathers Hypothesis <that there is Effectively> (as Mr Bayle affirms $^{325}$ ) a Compatibilitie supposed of a Power to Organize animals, with the want of Knowledge. $^{326}$ Since to the Production of such a Work as this, two things (according to my Father) must concur, that is, the Idea of

label: footnote
content: 319 In his Continuation, Bayle points out that if matter can act purposefully for ends (as Cudworth proposes), this lends support to atheism insofar as matter might conceivably act by itself, i.e. the apparent purposefulness of the material world might be explained without recourse to God.

label: footnote
content: $^{320}$ Deletion in manuscript: '(in effect)'.

label: footnote
content: 321 Masham translates remarks from Bayle's critique of Cudworth: 'Dieu . . . a pû donner aux créatures une faculté de produire d'excellens ouvrages séparée de toute conoissance' (Oeuvres, vol. iv, p. 183).

label: footnote
content: 322 Masham denies Bayle's assertion: 'Vous devez donc avouer qu'il n'y a point de liaison necessaire entre la faculté de produire d'excellens ouvrages, & l'idée de leur essence, & de la maniere de les produire' (Bayle, Oeuvres, vol. iv, p. 183).

label: footnote
content: $^{323}$ Cudworth asserts that 'the Plastick Nature essentially depends upon Mind or Intellect, and could not possibly be without it' (True Intellectual System, p.171).

label: footnote
content: 324 Masham paraphrases Bayle, who asks: 'Pourquoi donc prétendez-vous que ces deux choses ne peuvent pas être séparées dans la Nature, & que la Nature ne peut avoir d'elle-même ce qu'ont, selon vous, les êtes plastiques par un don de Dieu?' (Bayle, Oeuvres, vol. iv, p. 183).

label: text
content: But Mr Bayle argues, That if Plastick Natures have no Intire Efficiencie of theire Owne, they will then need such Perpetual direction as is ascribed to Material Causes; and so my Fathers Hypothesis will be but in the same case with the Cartesian. $^{327}$ Mr Bayle Affirms this; but (as I think) he no where Proves it: All that he offers amounting (as I have alreadie observed) onelie to a beging of this Question, that God cannot make a Creature to Act but either from Ideas of what it dos; or else by such Perpetual Direction as that of the Cartesian Material Causes. Whence he rightly infers that if Plastick Natures Act not by Ideas which they have, as it is presumed the Destroying Angel did do in distinguishing the Egyptians from the Israelites and so on: they then must Act as He supposes Fire (had it so pleased God) might have done, in Destroying the First Born of Egypt; that is, by Gods Perpetual applying and directing it. $^{328}$ But to Any Ones bare Assertion that a thing is Inconceivable, it is surely answer sufficient that Others find it not to be so. Though my Father has given some instances which he thinks prove the possibilitie of such a Manner of Action as he ascribes to Plastick Natures; that is, in the Operations of Habits: as (for Example) those of Singing and Danceing: which shall oftentimes direct the Motions of the Body, or Voice, without any consideration of what the next Note, or Motion should be. $^{329}$

label: text
content: I beg Leave here to trespass so much farther on Your Patience, as to observe to you one thing wherin Mr Bayle is mistaken in <reference to> this matter, which has not been taken notice of, and that is, in a presumeing that my Father designed in introduceing his Hypothesis, to oppose the Modern Cartesians: $^{330}$ whereas He (not understanding French) did not know that the Modern Cartesians differed so $<\mathrm{m u c h}>^{331}$ from theire Master as to hold that

label: footnote
content: $^{327}$ Bayle, Oeuvres, vol. iv, p. 183.

label: footnote
content: 328 Bayle refers to this same biblical example (from Exodus 12:23) in his critique of Cudworth (see Bayle, Oeuvres, vol. iv, pp. 184-5).

label: footnote
content: 329 Masham paraphrases Cudworth's words in his True Intellectual System. There he explains how plastic nature can act for the sake of ends, yet be devoid of consciousness itself, with reference to 'Habits, particular those Musical ones, of Singing, Playing upon Instruments, and Dancing. Which Habits direct every motion of the Hand, Voice, and Body, and prompt them readily, without any Deliberation or Studied Consideration, what the next following Note or Motion should be' (Cudworth, True Intellectual System, p. 157).

label: footnote
content: 330 By 'Modern Cartesians', Masham evidently has in mind the occasionalists, Nicolas Malebranche and his followers, those theorists who maintain that God is the only true causal agent in the natural world.

label: text
content: God was the Immediate Efficient Cause of all the Effects of nature and the Hypothesis of the Plastick Nature (produced by him for the acquiting from the suspicion of Atheism some who held a Plastick Life distinct from the Animal) was very far from having the Cartesians in View; however they may find themselves conamed when the opinion of such is Condemned as held that God himself did All immediately in the Efformation and Organization of the Bodies of Animals, as well as the other phenomena: Which with the Opinion of all things coming to pass Fortuitously, my Father considered as the onely two Hypothesiss, which were opposed to that of Plastick Natures. $^{332}$

label: text
content: Now Mr Bayle (considering Perpetual Direction onelie in such a sense as makes God the Immediate Efficient cause of <all> the Effects of Nature) presumes that my Father is obliged to deny all Kind of Perpetual Direction to Plastick Natures; which (as I take it) he dos not: since (according to him) theire operations are always determined by the Ideas in the Divine Intellect; $^{333}$ and his Hypothesis opposes onely such Direction as makes God the Immediate Efficient Cause of all the Works of Nature. Plastick Natures being by him Substituted as the Agents or Executioners of the Divine Will and Pleasure. As $^{334}$ Perpetual Direction then is Understood, or may be Explained, it seems to me that Plastick Natures may be, and are by my Father (in what he says of them) both affirmed and denyed, to have Perpetual Direction: in which, if he talks Contradictiously, or Inconsistently it lies upon Mr Bayle to show that he dos so, stateing first rightly what is herein asserted by him.

label: text
content: I pretend not at all to be Positive in any thing which I have here ventured to say on so nice a subject, and so much above my Examination as not easilie to be set in a due Light by two so Acute and Extraordinarie Men as both Mr Le Clerc and Mr Bayle are. I onelie take the libertie breifly to suggest to you my Thoughts thereon to the end that I may learn from you how far they are Right.

label: text
content: The Last answer of Mr Le Clerc I have not yet read, his Civilitie in sending me one (which I heare has Miscarryed) having made me thus Long neglect buying it. But I am told that Mr Bayle will still reply: and that the Subject of the Controversie is by some thought to be by Mr Le Clercs answer too much enlarged <in> a Consideration of the Usefulness of the Hypothesis of

content: ## My Lady

label: text
content: I am very much obliged to you particularly for the share that you take in the loss we have suffered with the death of the Queen of Prussia. The affliction such an accident can cause is not one of the lesser passions whose acuity, one can generally say, reason can diminish only by some sort of diversion, but rather has enough power over the external actions of anyone accustomed to heeding it. You make me very happy, Madam, in allowing me to hope that we might see you here one day. Madam the Electress $^{335}$ would be delighted about it. The English language is so familiar to her that she loves to converse with people that speak it, but nothing would be more agreeable to her than

label: text
content: an English Lady whose intellect is as elevated as yours. I sent my response to Mr Bayle concerning his objections in the last edition of his Dictionary. Since both he and Mr Le Clerc have spoken of my system in their writings that appear in the Dutch Journals, I have seized the opportunity to include a small written clarification of it that will perhaps also be published in one of these journals. And since you touch upon the same subject in your letter, I would say to you, Madam, that in my opinion matter, even though it is devoid of consciousness, can act in a way that allows it to serve an end, without it needing to have a particular direction applied to it by God, or some other intelligence during the action; for one can conceive that God gave it first a structure which enables it to produce in time actions consistent with reason. Since our engineers, whose talents are so limited, can provide examples of this in certain circumstances, by means of machines that imitate reason, it is easy to infer that what is most beautiful in the artifices of man must be all the more so in the works of God, and that God, whose art infinitely surpasses our own, could obtain this effect in any kind of circumstance, without needing specific plastic natures or his own particular cooperation to the actual formation of animals. This is where my hypothesis differs from others. For I do not wish, with respect to natural things, to appeal to God's peculiar guidance, which could only be miraculous, nor have recourse to incorporeal plastic natures which would have no advantage over the machine. I would therefore say that bodies have in them plastic natures, but these natures are nothing other than their own machines, which produce excellent works without consciousness of what they do, because these Machines have been invented by a Master who is even more excellent. The plastic force is in the Machine, but the idea of what it does is in God. Hence, I deny any power to creatures whose possibility cannot be clearly conceived. And the formation of animals is all the more explicable, since it always comes from a preformation, that is to say, that there is always an animal of its form. Habitual actions too (like those that we perform in playing the harpsichord, without thinking about everything that we are doing) confirm what I have just said, namely that the Machine is capable of acting reasonably without knowing it, when it has been so predisposed by a rational substance. For one would not play so well without thinking enough about what one was doing, if one had not given oneself beforehand the disposition necessary for that, which is the result of having thought about it in the process of learning to play. When I say that the peculiar guidance of God is miraculous, I distinguish it from that universal guidance whereby God preserves things according to the laws of nature. But

label: text
content: guidance is peculiar or miraculous when what is being done is not consistent with these laws, and hence is not explicable in terms of our distinct notions of created things. For example, a body in the void could not follow a circular trajectory without peculiar guidance. And if the planets moved in the void, they would have to be led by an assisting intelligence, because—naturally and following the mathematical laws—a body left to itself would move along the tangent to the circle and away from its centre as soon as it is at liberty to do so. I therefore believe that all the difficulties we have created for ourselves concerning plastic natures are overcome in the way I have just explained. I submit this explanation to your judgment, and yet I recognize that in Mr Cudworth's system, where plastic natures are directed by the ideas of God, Atheists find no retaliatory means to elude the argument which draws on the marvels of nature, any more than in the system of occasional causes, which demands this peculiar guidance everywhere. It is true that I find it more philosophical to explain the formation of animals, like the rest, by the machine of nature, but predisposed by divine wisdom; similarly, it is the mark of a more skilled worker to make a clock that works well with less aid from a peculiar guidance.

label: text
